entry.title: US import duty from Python: every tariff layer for an HTS code, free (pip install zentria-flow)
entry.summary:
If you sell physical products into the US, "what is the duty on this?" stopped having one answer. A cotton T-shirt from China doesn't pay its 16.5% MFN rate. It pays 36.5%, because two more tariffs sit on top. Christmas lights from China pay 45.5%; the same lights from Vietnam pay 20.5%. Spreadsheets get this wrong because the layers come from different legal programs, each with its own exemptions and dates. So we put our tariff engine behind a free API and wrapped it in a small Python package. pip install zentria-flow
No key, no account, no dependencies (standard library only). $ zentria-flow check 9405.31.00 CN HTS 9405.31.00 from CN (entry date 2026-11-20) Luminaires and lighting fittings ... not elsewhere specified or included MFN duty 8% Section …

entry.title: Batch background removal rarely fails because it's slow
entry.summary: our ways a batch goes to waste, and what a batch you can actually ship looks like. A 30-image batch dies at image 22. Or you get to image 6, the tab refreshes, and the first five results are gone. Accidents like these are routine in batch tools, and they have almost nothing to do with model quality. Batching stretches a task from seconds to tens of minutes, while a browser session is fragile: memory runs out, tabs get suspended, hands slip. The hard part of a batch tool is not how many images it accepts. It is what happens across those minutes when something goes wrong. One failure takes the whole batch with it Symptom: a single image fails and the batch stops. You hit retry, and it starts again from image one. Why: the queue is implemented as a loop plus one batch-level error state, so a …

entry.title: Run AWS SDK Tests in Your App's Language with One CLI
entry.summary:
An AWS Emulator gives your tests a local AWS API. Running an integration test still involves several steps: start the emulator, wait until it is ready, configure the SDK endpoint and certificate, then clean up when the test exits. awesome-emulator-cli wraps the test command you already use and manages that lifecycle. Python stays in pytest, Java in Maven, Rust in Cargo, Go in go test, and .NET in dotnet test. Node.js runs the CLI; your application stays in its native runtime. The sample repository includes a Python test that writes a value to S3 and reads it back. The client uses Boto3's normal environment-based configuration—there is no endpoint or certificate path in the test: from uuid import uuid4

entry.title: How AI Agents Adapt When Plans Break: Lessons from the Minecraft Experiment
entry.summary: What 50 AI agents did under pressure in Minecraft reveals how they'll actually behave in production systems. Fifty AI agents were dropped into a shared Minecraft survival world with one instruction: defeat the Ender Dragon. No playbook. No predefined roles. They had to figure it out, and fast. entry.title: Preventing Data Inconsistencies: Distributed Locking with Redis in Microservices
entry.summary: Modern microservices architectures empower rapid development and independent scaling, yet they introduce inherent complexities, particularly around shared resources. When multiple services concurrently access and modify the same piece of data, such as an inventory count, a payment balance, or a user profile, the risk of race conditions leading to data inconsistency is significant. Without proper synchronization mechanisms, your application can suffer from corrupted data, incorrect business logic, and severe financial consequences. This challenge is not theoretical; it's a real-world problem that leads to customer dissatisfaction, costly debugging, and eroded trust. entry.summary: A trivia round usually asks one question at a time. If you know the answer, you give it and move on. That design makes each clue an isolated test of recall. But what happens if a correct answer is no longer available later in the same run? An easy question becomes a resource-allocation decision: take the obvious answer now, or save it for a more restrictive clue. That is the small but consequential rule behind Kabloom game, a free daily browser trivia game built around seven checkpoints on a pixel-art volcano. You read a clue, type a name that fits, and climb when it is accepted. Once a name counts, it is spent for the rest of that game—even if it could have satisfied another clue. entry.title: Do you need bronze, silver and gold layers? Keep three things instead
entry.summary:
TL;DR. Probably not, if you are a startup with no data person. The three layers, called the medallion architecture, are a recommended practice, not a requirement, and the real work of the middle one, making two systems agree, can start as one mapping table. What you should not skip are three things that are often impossible to bring back later: an untouched copy of data as it arrived, one model that keeps history instead of overwriting it, and written definitions your coding agent can read. Add a layer when mappings multiply or a second consumer with different needs shows up, not before.
Illustration, not measured data. Data platforms often sort data into three layers. Bronze holds data as it arrived. Silver holds it cleaned and made to agree across sources. Gold holds tables shaped for r…

entry.title: Our WhatsApp AI receptionist isn't allowed to talk about money. It texts me first, and I answer with "A12 ok"
entry.summary: Most WhatsApp bots I've seen fail the same way: a customer asks "how much for X", the bot makes up a number or quotes an old one, and now the owner either honours a price he never set or looks like he's going back on his word. So when we built our own, the first rule was that the AI never states a price or agrees to a meeting on its own. The stack is n8n plus a self-hosted WhatsApp gateway (OpenWA), both on Railway, with Supabase as the memory. Here's how a message moves through it: It waits 20 seconds and only answers the newest message. People on WhatsApp send three short messages in a row, and answering each one separately looks robotic. entry.title: How we find viral moments in a 6-hour stream in 4 minutes
entry.summary: A GTA VI streamer this week sits in front of a camera for 6 to 10 hours. Somewhere in there are maybe ten moments worth a Short. Watching it back to find them takes longer than the stream. We built Clipjack to do that part, and the target was a 6-hour VOD in about 4 minutes of wall time. This is how the pipeline is shaped. The slow way is to run a model over every frame. A 6-hour 1080p60 VOD is about 1.3 million frames. Instead the ingest step cuts the stream into 15-minute pieces with a 30-second overlap (so a moment on a boundary isn't cut in half) and processes them four at a time. Each piece is read once and produces cheap signals, and the output is one per-second signal table for the whole stream. For streams, the streamer's voice is the best detector there is. entry.title: Draft a GitHub pull request in Claude Code with a /pr slash command
entry.summary:
If you keep pasting the branch diff and "write a PR title and body, then wait" into Claude Code, turn that prompt into a slash command. The file name becomes the command; $ARGUMENTS lets you name the base branch or add extra instructions. Save this as .claude/commands/pr.md: --- description: "Draft a GitHub pull request from the current branch" argument-hint: "[base branch | extra instructions]" ---
Draft a GitHub pull request for the current branch. Do not create it until I confirm.
1. Run `git status -sb`, `git log --oneline -15`, and `git diff origin/HEAD...HEAD` (or `main...HEAD` if `origin/HEAD` is missing). If there is no unique commit versus the base, stop and say so. 2. If I passed arguments (`$ARGUMENTS`), treat the first token as a base branch when it looks like one (`main`, `master`, `develop`, or `origin/...`). Treat the rest as extra instructions. 3. Propose a PR title and a body with a short summary, a test plan, and any follow-ups. Do not add AI attribution unless I ask. 4. Show the title and body and wait for me to confirm before running `gh pr create`. Never force-push, never merge, and never add reviewers I did not name.
Use it as /pr, /pr main, or /pr develop include a migration note. Slash commands are markdown files in .claude/commands. Claude Code injects the file as the prompt and replaces $ARGUMENTS with whatever you type after the command. Keeping "wait for confirm" and "never force-push or merge" in the command reduces unattended PR creation. Pair this with an "ask" permission rule for gh pr create if you also want a permissions bump. Commit the command file so every teammate gets the same workflow. Pair with a /commit command so the branch messages and the PR body stay consistent. I keep copy-ready Claude Code configs (CLAUDE.md templates, slash commands, hooks, permission rules) in Vildanden Agent Config. There's a free sample: https://justly-mia-429.rehost.page/

entry.title: How are you handling RTSP frame drops and queue backpressure in multi-camera video analytics pipelines?
entry.summary:
Hi all, We are currently architecting an edge-deployed video analytics service tasked with processing 8 simultaneous 1080p @ 25fps RTSP camera streams for real-time person/object detection on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin / RTX workstation. Our pipeline uses GStreamer with hardware-accelerated H.264 decoding feeding into a shared frame queue for batched YOLOv8/TensorRT inference. However, during high-activity periods, we observe buffer bloat and progressive stream desync: import cv2 init(self, rtsp_url, frame_queue): The Bottleneck: If we drop intermediate non-key frames (delta frames) when the inference queue fills, we experience decoding artifacts.
If we keep the queue synchronous, latency creeps up to 2.5–4.0 seconds behind live time within 10 minutes of runtime.
My Questions: What architectural pattern do you recommend for decoupling ingest from inference without accumulating buffer delay?
Are you relying on NVIDIA DeepStream SDK plugins (nvstreammux, nvinferserver), or rolling lightweight Python/C++ multiprocessing queues with shared memory (multiprocessing.shared_memory)?
Would love to hear how others handle multi-camera concurrency at the edge!

entry.title: Diese Woche haben mir zwei Tools etwas vorgeschlagen und es direkt abgeschickt.
entry.summary:
Diese Woche haben mir zwei Tools etwas vorgeschlagen und es direkt abgeschickt. Das dritte hat gefragt. Ich habe nur eins davon behalten. Der Unterschied lag nicht in der Qualität des Vorschlags, sondern im Moment davor: Vorschlag fertig – Freigabe fehlt. FOX WIZ ist genau um diese Grenze gebaut. Die App verbindet E-Mail, Kalender, Kontakte, Aufgaben und Dateien, liest ausschließlich die Dienste, die du freigibst, und legt danach fertige Dinge bereit: eine Antwort im Postfach, einen Terminvorschlag, eine Aufgabe mit Fälligkeit. Nichts davon verlässt das Gerät in Richtung anderer Menschen, bevor du bestätigt hast. Aktionen mit Außenwirkung warten. Spannend wird es bei der Frage, wo diese Grenze genau verläuft. Sortieren, zusammenfassen, Entwurf schreiben – geschenkt, darf laufen. Aber eine Terminzusage an drei Leute? Eine Antwort an den Vermieter? Ein Dokument, das einen Ordner wechselt, den andere sehen? Meine Arbeitsregel bisher: Alles, was den Posteingang anderer Leute erreicht, braucht einen Menschen davor. Alles, was nur meinen eigenen Bildschirm sortiert, nicht. Das ist erstaunlich schwer sauber zu ziehen, sobald Kalender und Aufgaben mitspielen – ein verschobener Termin ist lokal, eine Einladung ist es nicht. Wo ziehst du die Grenze? Nenne mir eine Aktion, die dein Tool ohne Rückfrage ausführen darf – und eine, bei der du sie nie erlauben würdest.
productivity #privacy #buildinpublic

entry.title: What Is LLM Throughput? Tokens per Second, Concurrency, and Batching
entry.summary: When teams evaluate how a large language model (LLM) will perform in production, two families of metrics come up repeatedly. One family describes latency: how quickly an individual request is served. The other describes throughput: how much total work the system can accomplish in a given period. Throughput is what determines whether a deployment can serve ten users or ten thousand, and it is the metric most directly tied to infrastructure cost per request. Yet it is frequently misunderstood, partly because the headline figure, "tokens per second," can mean several different things depending on whether you are counting one stream or the whole system. entry.title: Scale the Model, Scale the Harness: Unlocking a 2 Leap in Mathematical Reasoning
entry.summary: Originally published in Generative AI on Medium. I spent months building a system that wraps a language model in a checking loop so it can prove hard math theorems. Every step gets verified with real math tools, the system remembers what worked, and a second pass tries to break the proof before it counts. Then I tested it on 300 hard math problems, and the results surprised me: the setup around the model matters as much as the model itself. The harness is three things: A checking loop. Every intermediate claim is verified in code (SymPy, Z3, 50-digit mpmath). The solver works on a persistent scratchpad; a separate auditor runs in a fresh kernel and tries to kill the proof. Memory. After each problem, a reflection pass distills what worked into heuristics the system reuses, with zero weight…

entry.title: How IP Intelligence Helps Catch Account Takeovers in Real Time
entry.summary: A correct password no longer proves that the right person is logging in. Leaked credentials are traded in huge lists, and attackers use automated tools to try them across thousands of websites. When one works, the login looks completely normal: right username, right password, no failed attempts. So how do you tell a real customer from an attacker holding their password? Look at where the login is coming from. The login looks right, but the connection doesn’t Every login request comes with an IP address, and that address carries context. With an IP intelligence lookup at sign-in, you can compare each attempt against what’s normal for that user and spot the outliers. Unexpected location. When designing storage for large objects in GBase Database(GBase 8s), one distinction is easy to overlook: BLOB and CLOB are smart large objects, and they must be stored in an sbspace rather than an ordinary business dbspace. This is not just a naming convention. It affects table creation, storage planning, backup, and database recovery. A common mistake is to create a BLOB column and place the table directly in a regular business dbspace. entry.title: GBase Database: How to Read Both Sections of onstat -d for Storage Monitoring

entry.title: How to check your Rust port against the Python original (with five real bugs it caught)
entry.summary:
You rewrote a Python library in Rust. The benchmarks look great and the test suite is green. One question is left, and it is the one your users care about: does it still do exactly what the old code did? Your tests can't fully answer that. They check the inputs you thought of. The differences hide in the inputs nobody thought of. The good news is that a port comes with something most code never has: a complete specification. It's the old code. You don't need to read the Rust or reason about it. Run both versions on the same input and compare what comes back. Repeat until they disagree. Here is how to do that in practice, and five places it found real bugs. def same(input): return python_version(input) == rust_version(input)
Everything else is detail. Where do the inputs come from? How…

entry.title: OpenTelemetry Observability Patterns for Financial Research Dashboard Retrieval Pipelines
entry.summary: Short answer: for a financial research dashboard, the retrieval architecture should be a costed, traceable pipeline with observability for index freshness, evidence quality, and latency. That decision matters more than picking a fashionable vector store. The same design works for a property-management watcher that compares listing pages, where every unnecessary re-index is a direct operating cost. Make the signal explain the bill. Start with one trace per user question. Give the request a stable trace ID, then record query rewriting, candidate retrieval, reranking, context assembly, and generation as child spans. Each span should carry a small set of dimensions: corpus name, index version, filter count, candidate count, token estimate, and outcome. Keep document text and account identifier…

entry.title: Your full-page screenshot is 355px wide inside Claude

A full-page screenshot looks like the perfect thing to give a coding agent, since the whole page fits in one image. Claude never reads that image at the size you took it. The test below uses one capture of a long article page: 1270px wide at 2x, so the PNG is 2540 x 18410. Claude caps the long edge of every image at 2576px and keeps the aspect ratio. Body text that was 16px in the file lands at about 2.2px.

entry.title: perf_event_paranoid controls observability privilege, not process trust
entry.summary:
perf_event_paranoid controls observability privilege, not process trust
Performance monitoring can expose more than instruction counts. It can sample execution, collect stack traces, observe kernel behavior, and provide timing information that helps an attacker understand a target. Linux exposes a system-wide knob that limits what an unprivileged process may measure: perf_event_paranoid. The kernel documentation defines a useful scale. At -1, almost all events are open to all users. At 0 or higher, unprivileged users cannot use ftrace function tracepoints or raw tracepoints without CAP_PERFMON. At 1 or higher, CPU event access is restricted. At 2 or higher, kernel profiling is disallowed. The default is 2. A privileged process can still bypass the checks, so the setting is not a substitu…

Munchable's app reads a product label and tells you whether that product suits your gut. The part of it that improves most often is not the code, it is the ingredient data: new words, new spellings, new names for the same thing. Shipping that through the app stores would mean a release per data fix, so instead the app downloads a snapshot of it and keeps a copy on the device. That means I need an answer to a question that comes up more often than you would think: has this phone's copy gone stale? The answer is one number. max(updated_at) over every active row of both tables, as an epoch-ms decimal string. '0' when empty. One number for the whole snapshot.

entry.title: Electron Release Engineering: A Practical Guide to Versioning, CI Build Matrices, Update Channels, Artifact Integrity, and Safe Rollbacks
entry.summary: Shipping a web app mostly means deploying a new build to a server; users load the fresh code on their next request. An Electron release is the opposite: you produce native installers for Windows, macOS, and Linux, each signed and packaged for several architectures, host them somewhere a feed can read, keep update metadata in sync, and then decide which users actually move to which version. When something goes wrong, the fix is not a redeploy of one bundle — it is withdrawing or blocking a native build that may already be installed on thousands of machines. Two people typing in one paragraph is a distributed systems problem in an editor's clothes. Operational transformation send each edit to a central server that rewrites it against everything concurrent, so every client applies the same sequence. entry.title: Passive Intermodulation: The RF Spec That Fails After Installation
entry.summary: Passive intermodulation is the specification that most often disappears from a component RFQ — and then reappears as a failed system test. It is called passive because the parts that generate it have no active devices in them. A switch contact, a connector interface or a load can all behave as a weak nonlinear junction when two carriers are present. Two tones at f₁ and f₂ passing through a nonlinearity produce products at mf₁ ± nf₂. The third-order terms 2f₁−f₂ and 2f₂−f₁ are the dangerous ones because they land close to the original carriers and can fall inside the receiver band. A typical test applies two 20 W tones and measures the third-order product in dBc; a well-built path might be −150 dBc or better, while a dirty or loose interface can be 30–40 dB worse. The physical causes are mu…

entry.title: Your Android App Is Dying in the Background and You Don't Know Why
entry.summary: 509 timestamp gaps across 159 tracking sessions. That was the number we found when we finally audited what happens to our Android app when the OS kills it in the background. We run a workforce tracking app on 30 BYOD Android devices. The app needs to record GPS coordinates every few minutes, even when the screen is off. The problem is that Android doesn't want your app running in the background. Between Doze mode, OEM battery optimisations, user force-stops, and reboots, there are at least five distinct ways your app can die without your code ever seeing an exception. I wrote a preprint that formalises this into a measurement framework: a kill-cause taxonomy, an instrumentation specification, and a classification procedure. The paper and data are open access on Zenodo: DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.…

entry.title: Building Self-Updating AI Knowledge Systems with AWS
entry.summary: I explore event driven, auto-updating RAG systems that solves real day to day problems. This includes document syncing, versioning and ensuring correct answers from AI. Based on my experimentation on AI tax awareness system on Ethiopian tax laws and regulation. Creating Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) applications is one of the easiest ways to create AI applications that can leverage your organisational knowledge. One of the engineering challenges that can easily be overlooked is ensuring the AI will get the latest information. Event Driven Approach We can use AWS to create a solution that: 1. Stores our documents in Amazon S3. 2. Captures document events using Amazon EventBridge. 3. Processes events asynchronously using Amazon SQS. 4. Extracts, detects and processes document changes using AWS Lambda. 5. Creates embeddings and enables smart document search using Amazon Bedrock. 6. Stores our document embeddings in a vector database. 7. This ensures that only the specific document that has changed needs to be processed. Engineering Challenges It is interesting to think about how we can make sure this is reliable. We need to consider handling duplicate events, failures, document versions, removal of documents and incomplete sync. Why it Matters Whilst creating a RAG application is easy to do, creating a reliable, accurate and scalable knowledge base is very interesting.

entry.title: 19 Custom Lint Rules Killed Design-System Drift in Two Production Flutter Apps
entry.summary: Colors.red in a Flutter widget. Sounds harmless. In a production app with a design system, it's a landmine: one developer uses Colors.red, another uses Theme.of(context).colorScheme.error, and six months later your app ships with two shades of red on the same screen and nobody can explain why. We had this problem across two production Flutter codebases (105K LOC and 59K LOC). Instead of writing a style guide nobody reads, we wrote 19 custom lint rules using the custom_lint framework. 13 are org-wide (published as kx_lints on pub.dev). 6 are project-specific. I wrote a preprint measuring the results: DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24263596. Design-system drift is when developers bypass your theme and use hardcoded values. In Flutter, the most common forms are: Colors.red instead of Theme.of(context).c…

entry.title: What Makes a Technology Project Trustworthy?
entry.summary: A technology project can look impressive in a demo and still fail when real users depend on it. Before choosing AI, blockchain, or a conventional database, I would ask three questions. First, can we explain where the data comes from and who is allowed to modify it? Second, can someone independently verify an important result? Third, what happens when the system fails, an input is incorrect, or a user needs a correction? These questions influence architecture, testing, access control, monitoring, and maintenance. For blockchain projects, immutability does not guarantee that the original information is true. For AI projects, fluent output does not guarantee accuracy. Trustworthy software needs evidence, accountability, and clear limitations. Discussion: Which technical decision has most improved trust in a system you've built? Suggested tags: #softwaredevelopment #blockchain #ai #architecture

entry.summary: InfraGuard Engineering Devlog, part 6 of 6. On November 12, five commits went into InfraGuard's rollup worker. Retention cleanup was not completing, a drain path had replayed data, and the worker blocked sensor inserts. The common theme was a mismatch between database work and process lifetime. entry.title: A repaired sensor made our dashboard take 28 seconds to load
entry.summary: InfraGuard Engineering Devlog, part 5 of 6. Restoring a stopped sensor on October 30 made telemetry healthier and the console slower. Recorded cold-cache tests averaged 13.3 seconds for the first view and reached 28.5 seconds. A weak-TLS aggregation was responsible. Recent 24-hour TLS data had grown to 3.01 million of 11.67 million rows. The optimizer changed its access plan; one query took 13–36 seconds. An index covering time and TLS version let this query read the index alone. The recorded online build took 82 seconds and added 353 MB. The aggregation then completed in about 1.8 seconds. We also precomputed the score every four minutes rather than making the first viewer pay the cold-query cost. Improving a query and removing expensive computation from a request path are separate fixes.…

entry.title: Recovering Logistics User Reminders — 4 Wrong Cron Expression and Timezone Safeguards
entry.summary:
TL;DR
For logistics reminders, make a short, fixed-rate scheduler discover due rows in UTC, claim each reminder with a durable delivery key, and let a retry worker deliver the outbound webhook. A cron expression should trigger discovery; it should never be the only record that a reminder was owed. This design survives a wrong timezone, a missed run, pause and resume, and a few seconds of jitter without turning recovery into duplicate delivery. I have been paged for both sides of this failure: a job that never fired and a retry that delivered twice. The invariant from those incidents is blunt: schedule time decides eligibility; durable state decides whether work may run. If the scheduler owns both decisions, its clock mistake becomes a customer-visible data mistake. Start by separating a …

entry.title: Will this LLM run on my laptop? The memory math to do before you download
entry.summary: The usual way people pick a local model goes like this. A model is trending, you pull 18 GB of weights over a slow connection, you start it, and it types four words a second while your fans spin up. entry.title: What Is OTP SMS? How Mobile Verification Works
entry.summary: An OTP SMS is a text message carrying a one-time password: a short random code that works once and expires within minutes. Mobile verification uses that code to show that someone controls a phone number right now. It proves access to the number, not who the person is. This guide follows one code from your server to a handset, works out how many digits and tries you can safely allow, and explains why OTPs fail before they reach the handset. entry.title: Packaged WriteFreely as a one-click Railway template — here's what self-hosting a blog actually costs
entry.summary: I kept seeing agents and humans spin up WriteFreely manually — clone the repo, generate keys, wrestle the SQLite-to-Postgres migration, configure federation — and give up before their first post federated. So I packaged the whole thing as a one-click Railway deploy: https://github.com/INAPP-Mobile/writefreely The concrete detail I'm proud of: the template generates the admin and app keys at deploy time with openssl rand inside the start script, so nobody ever commits a config with default secrets. Federation (ActivityPub) is enabled out of the box, which is the part most people botch — the site and open federation flags plus a proper instance domain are the difference between a blog that talks to the fediverse and one that silently doesn't. What it costs the operator: SQLite works fine and is the zero-config default, but the moment you want more than one replica or real concurrent writes, you're migrating to Postgres, and WriteFreely's schema doesn't make that a one-liner. I documented the migration path in the README rather than hiding it. Running your own instance also means you're the moderator — federation brings spam registrations, and the blocklist is on you. It's a small thing — a template, not a product — but it removes the three steps where everyone I watched quit.

Docker OCI runtime error container_linux mkdir /proc is a search people arrive with rather than a line the runtime prints, and knowing that is most of the fix. What runc actually emits when a container fails over /proc is a rootfs mount refusal, naming a path inside the container rootfs and a reason, and the reason is what decides whether you are looking at a privilege problem, a nesting problem or a mount you should not have asked for.
runc guards the container /proc before mounting anything. The refusal names the rootfs path, not the host one. entry.title: 'Agentic Search Architecture: Five Patterns That Survive Production'
entry.summary: Summary: The reasoning loop is the cheap part. What separates a working agentic search system from a demo is the control loop around it: typed tools, context isolation, budgets, and an evaluator that can send work back. The gain is real and measured. Agentic retrieval improves nDCG at 10 by 8.7 points using the same embedding model as standard retrieval. The cost is real too. entry.title: What actually happens to your backups during a ransomware run
entry.summary: It is 2am and a file server that has been idle for hours starts writing hard — .docx to .docx.locked, one file after another, as fast as the disk will go. Somewhere in that list is the folder your backup job finished writing to earlier that night. Nothing in that sequence was aimed at your backup. It was simply reachable. That distinction matters, because it is the whole reason "we have backups" so often turns out to be true and useless on the same morning. In the incident write-ups I've read over the years, the backup is almost never destroyed in a separate, dramatic second act. It goes down in the first pass, as ordinary traffic, and nobody notices until someone tries to restore. Ransomware doesn't know your file names. It enumerates what the machine can see: local volumes, mapped drives…

Then I did the same for each step of my AI workflow, from the spec (the text that describes what the code should do) to the commit. In the garden, each step has its own number, and the ideas that didn't pay off are there too. There is one note just for what I still don't know, because the study is small, comes from a few projects, and nobody outside has checked it. And there is a step-by-step to repeat the measurement on your own project. "A digital garden is a site of linked notes that the author keeps tending over time. It accepts unfinished notes and shows it, with a badge for how well each one is proven." If you want to take a look: Digital-Garden 🇧🇷 Eu medi isso junto com o Claude, fiz pesquisas e testes, e criei um jardim sobre se os testes pegam erro de verdade. A ideia é simples: um teste pode passar e ainda assim ser fraco. Para saber o quanto, estraguei o código de propósito e contei quantos erros os testes deixaram passar. Depois fiz o mesmo com cada passo do meu fluxo de trabalho com IA, da spec (o texto que descreve o que o código deve fazer) até o commit. No jardim, cada passo tem o seu número, e as ideias que não compensaram também estão lá. Tem uma nota só com o que eu ainda não sei, porque o estudo é pequeno, vem de poucos projetos e ninguém de fora conferiu. E tem um passo a passo para repetir a medida no seu projeto. "Jardim digital é um site de notas ligadas entre si, que o autor continua cuidando com o tempo. Ele aceita nota inacabada e mostra isso, com um selo de quanto cada uma está provada." entry.title: iPhone voice memos are M4A, here's how to get MP3s out of them
entry.summary: Voice memos, WhatsApp audio you saved, screen recordings of a call: on an iPhone almost all of it ends up as M4A or MOV. That's fine inside Apple's apps, but the moment you need to upload a recording to a form, a car stereo, an older MP3 player or a podcast host that wants MP3, it gets awkward. A few practical notes from dealing with this a lot: 1. Get the file out of the Voice Memos app first. Open the memo, tap the three dots, then "Save to Files". Now it's a normal .m4a file you can pick from any browser upload button. 2. Don't go above the source quality. Voice Memos records AAC at roughly 64-128 kbps depending on your "Audio Quality" setting. Exporting that as a 320 kbps MP3 only makes the file bigger. 128 kbps is plenty for speech; 96 kbps mono is fine for meeting notes. 3. For videos, you only want the audio track. Screen recordings and camera videos are MOV files. Converting them straight to MP3 drops the video and usually shrinks the file by 90% or more. 4. Trim silence before converting. Cutting the dead air at the start in the Voice Memos editor saves a second re-encode later. 5. Rename before sharing. "2026-11-14 client call.mp3" beats "New Recording 47.mp3" when it lands in someone else's inbox. For the conversion itself you don't need an app: we wrote up how to turn iPhone voice memos into MP3 straight from Safari, and the M4A to MP3 converter it uses runs in the browser with no sign-up. (Disclosure: it's our project.) What do you usually need MP3 for these days: uploads, car audio, or something else?

entry.title: Five checks for agent memory before using it in production
entry.summary: This article was prepared with AI assistance and reviewed by its author. A memory feature needs an acceptance test, not just a successful retrieval demo. Start with one small task whose answer you can check. Record its inputs, expected answer and permissions before enabling memory. Then try five cases: Recall: save a useful project fact, start a new session and check whether the agent retrieves the right source. Correction: replace that fact with a newer decision. Check that the agent uses the correction and exposes the old note as superseded. Missing context: ask about an unstored detail. The agent should expose the gap instead of treating a guess as remembered evidence. Isolation: repeat the question in a separate test workspace. Check that another workspace's private notes do not appear. Deletion: remove the test note and check retrieval again, including any application cache involved in the workflow. Run the same task without memory as a baseline. Keep a small results table with the case, expected result, retrieved evidence, actual answer and pass or failure. Repeat after changing extraction, retrieval or retention behavior. This is a proposed evaluation procedure, not a benchmark result. It tests whether memory helps the particular workflow while preserving correction, permissions and deletion controls. Original article: Read the original resource.

entry.title: Hydrogen spectrum lines from Bohr's model: Balmer wavelengths in JavaScript
entry.summary:
Bohr's model of hydrogen gives every spectral line of the atom from one formula, and you can reproduce the visible Balmer lines in a few lines of JavaScript. Below I compute the wavelengths of the lines you see in a hydrogen lamp and check the photon energy. (I build PractiSci, which has a free Bohr hydrogen lab.) 1/λ = R (1/n_f² − 1/n_i²), where R = 1.0968 × 10⁷ m⁻¹. Electrons falling to n = 2 give the visible Balmer series. Energy levels are Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV. const R = 1.0968e7; const nm = (nf, ni) => 1e9 / (R * (1 / nf ** 2 - 1 / ni ** 2));
for (const ni of [3, 4, 5, 6]) console.log(ni, '->2', nm(2, ni).toFixed(1), 'nm');
Transition Wavelength Colour
3 → 2 (Hα) 656.5 nm red
4 → 2 (Hβ) 486.3 nm blue-green
5 → 2 (Hγ) 434.2 nm violet
6 → 2 (Hδ) 410.3 nm violet
These match the measured Balmer lines. The same function gives 121.6 nm for the Lyman 2 → 1 line (ultraviolet) and 1876 nm for the Paschen 4 → 3 line (infrared), so only the Balmer series is visible. The 3 → 2 jump releases E₃ − E₂ = −1.51 − (−3.40) = 1.89 eV. The wavelength is λ = 1240 / E nm = 1240 / 1.89 ≈ 656 nm, the same red line. Its lines end on n = 2 and have energies of about 1.9 to 3.0 eV, which fall in the visible range. The Lyman lines are more energetic (ultraviolet) and the Paschen lines less (infrared). 13.6 eV, the energy to take the electron from n = 1 to infinity. In the free Bohr hydrogen lab you excite the atom and watch the lines appear. More Class 12 physics labs are in the labs list.

entry.title: Domótica DIY con ESP32 vs enchufes e interruptores inteligentes comerciales: qué sale más a cuenta
Orbital speed, escape speed and the square root of 2: a satellite calculator in JavaScript
entry.summary:
The speed a satellite needs to stay in orbit and the speed needed to escape Earth are linked by one number, √2. You can check it in a few lines of JavaScript, and the same code gives the period of the ISS and of a geostationary satellite. (I build PractiSci, which has a free satellite-orbits lab.) Orbital speed at height h: v = √(GM/(R + h)). Escape speed: v_esc = √(2GM/(R + h)). Orbital period: T = 2π√((R + h)³/GM). const G = 6.674e-11, Me = 5.972e24, Re = 6.371e6; const orbitV = (h) => Math.sqrt(G * Me / (Re + h)); const period = (h) => 2 * Math.PI * Math.sqrt((Re + h) ** 3 / (G * Me)); const escape = (h) => Math.sqrt(2 * G * Me / (Re + h));
Orbit Orbital speed Period Escape speed
Near the surface 7.91 km/s 1.41 h 11.19 km/s
ISS (400 km) 7.67 km/s 1.54 h 10.85 km/s
Geostationary (35,786 km) 3.07 km/s 23.93 h 4.35 km/s
The ratio escape/orbital is 1.4142 at every height, which is √2. That is why a satellite already has about 70% of the speed it would need to leave Earth altogether. Its period must equal one sidereal day, 23.93 h. Solving T = 2π√(r³/GM) for r gives r ≈ 42,164 km from the centre of the Earth, which is 35,786 km above the surface. Then the satellite stays over the same point on the equator. No. It cancels, so a tiny satellite and a space station at the same height have the same speed. They are in free fall around the Earth, not beyond gravity. Gravity at 400 km is still about 89% of its surface value. The free satellite orbits lab lets you change the height and see the speed and period, and the work, energy and power guide covers the energy side.

entry.summary: On 10 November 2026 Meituan published the LongCat-2.5 open weights on Hugging Face under the MIT licence: a 1.6 trillion parameter mixture-of-experts model with about 48 billion parameters active per token, in a 3.56 TB repository. You open an old assembly — mscorlib, say, or a netstandard facade — ask your tools for System.ValueTuple, and the type is listed but has no code. It is not a stub the compiler forgot to fill in. entry.title: A checklist for using a health AI safely, and for building one that earns your trust
entry.summary: After weeks of reading about scribes, answer engines, chart copilots, patient assistants, regulators and data, the same seven questions keep coming back. They work two ways: as a checklist if you use a health AI, and as a spec if you build one. 1. Does it show where the answer came from? 2. Does it tell you when it does not know? 3. Does it say what it will not do? 4. Who pays for it? 5. What happens to your data? 6. Is there a way to a human? 7. Are the limits published, including the bad numbers? If you build health AI, copy the list. Write each answer as a sentence on your site and as a test in your code. The ones you cannot answer in one sentence are your next tickets. Limits and test results for my own project are at tabibu.health/trust. I post short videos in this series on LinkedIn and TikTok; come say hi. General information, not medical advice.

entry.title: AI won't replace engineers
entry.summary:
I've been building a product at work for 6 months. Every line of code was written by AI. It still isn't finished. People keep telling me AI makes building software easy. That hasn't been my experience. AI is very fast at writing code. But typing code was never the slow part. The slow part is deciding what to build, keeping the design coherent across hundreds of prompts, and remembering why you chose something three weeks ago. The AI doesn't carry that for you. It will also happily generate two pieces that quietly contradict each other, then help you debug the mess it made. Fast code means fast problems. A big share of these 6 months has gone into reviewing, untangling, re-prompting and fixing things that looked fine when they were generated. I'm not going back to working without it. It's a great tool. But it changed where the work sits for me: less typing, more judgment. Design, review, debugging, trade-offs. My own project tells the same story. Publlsh, the tool I'm posting this from, is built the same way. I started it in February, about 9 months ago, and it's still not complete. So no, I don't think AI replaces engineers. If anything, the people who understand how systems fit together get the most out of it. Anyone else building with mostly AI-generated code? I'd like to hear what caught you off guard.
AI #SoftwareEngineering #BuildInPublic

entry.title: OpenQodex: a separate AI reviewer that checks agent-written code before you push
entry.summary:
OpenQodex
Review after the push is too late, and a review by the same agent that wrote the code is not a review. OpenQodex puts the check in between. It runs before you push, on the commits you have not pushed plus everything uncommitted. First, 22 built in scanners check the changed lines for secrets, security problems, vulnerable dependencies, and lint. Then a separate Claude Code or Codex process reviews the change, quoting every finding against the code. If a stage did not run, the report says Review incomplete instead of passing. It needs no account or API key of its own, and it runs on your Claude Code or Codex login. Version 0.18.0 shipped on 11 November 2026, and the repo now has 1,157 stars under Apache-2.0. What you get A pre-push check that covers unpushed commits and uncommitted work, not just pull requests A separate reviewer process with no memory of the session that wrote the code An honest receipt: every finding quoted against the code, and Review incomplete when a stage did not run Install with npx openqodex init, on Node 22, macOS or Linux, with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Cline or Goose as the host Try it on a branch you already trust first, and let it earn the push gate before you make it blocking. Repo: https://github.com/openqodex/openqodex What would you use OpenQodex for first? Reviewing a change before pushing Adding the push gate to my repo Running the scanners only Trying the demo repo first Vote in the comments. If you found OpenQodex interesting, I write about tools like this every week in The AI-Native Engineering Leader, what actually works for engineering leaders building with AI agents, and what to skip.

CVE-2026-126190: Polynomial-Time Denial of Service in Soup Sieve CSS Descendant Combinator
Vulnerability ID: CVE-2026-126190 CVSS Score: 7.5 Published: 2026-11-13 CVE-2026-126190 (GHSA-mmhr-3c5m-f64f) is an inefficient algorithmic complexity vulnerability (CWE-407) in Soup Sieve, the default CSS selector library integrated into Beautiful Soup 4. In versions prior to 4.0, evaluating CSS selectors that contain descendant combinators (whitespace between compound selectors) executes an unmemoized upward traversal of the document tree. When evaluated against deeply nested HTML or XML documents, the time complexity scales polynomially at O(n^(k+1)), where n is the tree depth and k is the number of descendant combinators. entry.title: Testing Client Timeout Behavior
entry.summary: Quick answer: A timeout is the client deciding to stop waiting, not a response from the server, so test it with fixed mock latency that lands just before and just after the threshold. Assert that the call aborts with the right error, the loading state resets, timers and in-flight work are cleaned up, retries follow a backoff schedule, and a response that arrives after the abort is ignored rather than applied twice. If you only test the fast, successful call, the slow path is still untested. When the threshold passes, the server may still be processing the request, which is why a blind retry can create a duplicate side effect. entry.title: The follow-up I lost in a Slack thread (and the one-page tracker that would have caught it)
entry.summary:
I once let a warm “let’s start next month” message die in a Slack thread I forgot to star. The client was real. The budget was real. I had quoted, they had said yes-in-spirit, and then a product launch ate both of our weeks. When I finally remembered to nudge them, the thread was buried under 200 unread messages and they had already hired someone who followed up on a Tuesday. The fix was not “check Slack more.” It was a single place that answered three questions every Friday in under ten minutes: Who is open? — lead, discovery, proposal sent, waiting, active, won, lost
When did I last touch them? — a date, not a vibe
What is the next visible action? — one verb: send proposal, nudge, send invoice, schedule kickoff, mark lost I keep it boring on purpose: a Clients list, a Pipeline board (Lead → Discovery → Proposal → Won / Active / Lost), and an Invoices table (Draft → Sent → Due → Overdue → Paid). Notion works. A Markdown table works. A spreadsheet works. The tool matters less than looking at it once a week before you open chat. You can steal the shape today: make three columns (name / last touch / next action), dump every half-alive lead into it, and set one 15-minute Friday review. No kit required. Want a free taste of the paperwork stack first? Five one-pagers (rate card, kickoff questions, change-order, three client emails, tax habits) sit in a pay-what-you-want sampler: https://lulupearl0.gumroad.com/l/freelance-starter-sampler Need a clean deposit/final invoice PDF with no signup? https://eclectic-cactus-07703e.netlify.app/ If you want the Notion-ready Markdown tables + a CSV import starter + a weekly dashboard checklist in one ZIP, I bundled it as a $19 Freelance Client Tracker (no monthly SaaS): https://lulupearl0.gumroad.com/l/freelance-client-tracker Building in public: store has views, revenue is still $0. Soft promo stays honest. If you use a simpler tracker ritual that actually sticks, I would love to hear it.

entry.title: Five Checks Before Calling a Web3 Prototype Production-Ready
entry.summary:
A successful smart contract deployment is not the same as a production-ready application. Before release, I would want the team to demonstrate five things: Network identity. Confirm the expected chain ID, deployment address, contract bytecode, and configuration.
Reproducibility. Show that another developer can repeat the deployment and verification process in a controlled environment.
Failure handling. Test RPC timeouts, failed transactions, delayed confirmations, and unavailable external services.
Access control. Verify privileged operations, key management, permission boundaries, and recovery procedures.
Data integrity. Document how off-chain information is collected, validated, and connected to on-chain records.
These checks do not guarantee security. They make important assumptions visible and create a starting point for independent testing. A useful technical write-up should include the environment, test procedure, expected result, observed result, and known limitations. Which of these checks has revealed the most unexpected problems in your projects?

entry.title: Remember your 404s until the next deploy
entry.summary: Most caching advice is about remembering things that exist. This one is about remembering things that don't. If you serve static files from object storage or a bucket behind a worker, every request for a missing file still costs you a lookup. Browsers ask for favicon.ico at the root even if you never had one. Bots probe for paths that were never there. Old links point at files that got renamed. Each of those is a round trip to storage that ends in the same answer: not here. I added a small negative cache for this to a thing I run, and the rule that made it safe was simple: a 404 is only true until the next deploy. The set of files can only change when you deploy. entry.title: Debloat Doesn't Stick. That's the Entire Product.
entry.summary: Last month I wrote about debloating my Google TV Streamer over ADB. The lesson there was disable, don't uninstall — keep the road back. This is the same problem on Windows, except Windows has a second failure mode the streaming devices don't, and it's the one that makes people say "I removed that already." This is the fact the whole design hangs on. Windows keeps two copies of any app that ships with the OS: the copy installed into your user account, and the copy baked into the system image that gets installed for new user accounts. They're separate things with separate removal commands, and the command that lists them isn't the one that deletes them. Remove only the per-user package and it comes back. Not immediately — for the next account created on that machine, and sometimes after an u…

entry.title: The model that writes a page shouldn't be the one that signs it off
entry.summary: My name is Hrithic Rajpurohit, and I work on the engineering team at Produsa Labs. We built Produsa, an AI website builder made for India, so I should tell you that before I describe how the build pipeline works. A website build is not one task. Research, brand, copy, layout, code and a final check all ask different things of a model. If the whole job goes through a single model, the writing, the design sense and the engineering quality all settle at whatever that model is average at. Produsa instead sends each job to the model that does it best. The ones we use are Claude, OpenAI, Gemini, xAI/Grok and Kimi. We have not published a map of which model takes which step, so I will not invent one here. The useful part is the idea: pick the model for the job, not one model for the whole product. We also added a second, separate pass. After a page is written and designed, a different AI reviews it against a written design rulebook. The first pass can look finished and still miss the brief, repeat a layout, or drift from the brand. That review only works if the rulebook is specific enough to fail. A vague "make it look good" rule just gets a yes. What I would tell another team doing this: write the bar down before you hook up the reviewer. If the only standard lives in someone's head, the review pass has nothing firm to argue with. If you have tried a reviewer model on generated UI or copy, I am curious what you put in the rulebook, and what it still lets through. This article was drafted with AI assistance and then checked by me. I can stand behind the facts above.

entry.title: The AI Code Maintenance Myth: Why 'Unmaintainable' Isn't the Real Problem
entry.summary: Originally published on tamiz.pro. Somewhere between the first 'AI writes a sorting algorithm' demo and today's million-line codebases, a comforting narrative hardened into conventional wisdom: AI-generated code is unmaintainable. It's too clever, too dense, too inconsistent. Reviewers dread it. Junior engineers can't read it. It's a ticking debt bomb. This narrative is wrong — not because AI code is maintainable, but because the diagnosis is. 'Unmaintainable' is a label we apply when we can't find the intent behind a change. AI doesn't fail at producing maintainable code; it fails at producing code that carries intent. Those are different problems, and confusing them has led teams to waste enormous effort reviewing line-level style when they should be fixing the architectural and organiza…

entry.title: I built a 15-tool PDF suite running 100% on-chain with React and Motoko
entry.summary: Hey everyone, Most web-based PDF tools upload your private files to a random backend server just to merge a couple of pages or add a signature. I wanted to see what it would look like to build an all-in-one PDF utility suite that runs completely serverless on the Internet Computer Protocol (ICP). After a lot of trial and error configuring the UI and backend logic, I finally wrapped up VaultyPDF. Instead of building just a basic file converter, I packed 15+ everyday document utilities into a single dark-mode dashboard: Core file handling: Merging, splitting, compressing, and page cropping. Security & privacy: Permanent document redaction and on-chain e-signatures. Tracking: Decentralized user metadata and file state tracking handled directly through Motoko canisters (main.mo). Frontend: React with a clean, dark-mode SaaS dashboard layout. Backend: Motoko canisters running on ICP for serverless execution without traditional cloud databases. Setting up the frontend routing, dark-mode components, and Motoko canister connections from scratch took way longer than I expected. Since a lot of solo devs and indie hackers want to build micro-SaaS apps on ICP without spending weeks on boilerplate layout code, I cleaned up the repo and packaged it as a starter template. If you are building on ICP or just want to save yourself 100+ hours of frontend and canister setup, you can check out the full source code bundle here: 👉 Grab the VaultyPDF React + Motoko Boilerplate on Gumroad Would love to hear what you guys think about running heavy document workflows on-chain, or if anyone else here is building SaaS tools with Motoko!

entry.title: Private SaaS Document Storage with Signed Links and 1-Day Retention (Trade-offs)
entry.summary: Private files change the storage decision. For a SaaS app holding invoices and PDFs, the useful default is a private bucket, an application-owned document index, and a short-lived presigned URL for each download. Keep retention and deletion in your database and lifecycle policy; do not make a public URL the record of truth. Short answer: Infrai fits this workflow when access stays private and signed links are enough, while Amazon S3, Cloudflare R2, DigitalOcean Spaces, and Backblaze B2 remain better choices when you need public objects, versioning, object lock, or mature replication controls. Uploading a file is the easy part. entry.title: Why Spreadsheets Corrupt CSV Files (And Why Plain-Text Matters)
entry.summary:
CSV files are the backbone of data exchange—simple, universal, and incredibly versatile. It's not flashy, it's not trendy, and yet it is everywhere. But if CSV files are so simple, important, and universal, why do they feel so painful to work with?
The origins of the CSV file date back to the early days of computing when simplicity was key. Developers needed a lightweight, platform-agnostic way to store and share tabular data, and the CSV was born. CSV stands for Comma-Separated Values. At its core, it's a plain text file where data is organized into rows and columns, with commas (or other delimiters like semicolons, tabs, or pipes) acting as the dividers. For example: Name, Age, Favorite Food Alice, 30, Pizza Bob, 25, Sushi

entry.title: Hook0 service tokens need attenuation before they leave the backend
entry.summary:
Hook0 service tokens need attenuation before they leave the backend
Hook0 is a webhook delivery service that can be self-hosted or used as a managed service. Its API creates applications, subscriptions, event types, and delivery records. Service tokens authenticate automated API calls on behalf of an organization. The service-token model is more capable than a simple application API key. Hook0 documents service tokens as organisation-scoped by default, with Biscuit-based offline attenuation. entry.title: How to install a Codex plugin: CLI, app and GitHub repos
entry.summary:
Disclosure: I run PickAPlugin, an independent catalog of ChatGPT and Codex plugins. This is adapted from our guide on the same topic. There are basically three ways a plugin gets onto your machine: the built-in directory, a GitHub repo that ships a marketplace, or a folder you made yourself. Here's each one. In the Codex app or ChatGPT desktop app, open Plugins, search, open the plugin and hit install. In the CLI, start codex and type /plugins. Plugins in the OpenAI tab are the ones OpenAI curates, so this is the low-risk route. Most community plugins live in a repo that has a .agents/plugins/marketplace.json (or the older .claude-plugin/marketplace.json). You add the repo as a marketplace once, then install by name: codex plugin marketplace add owner/repo codex plugin list codex plugin add plugin-name@marketplace-name
The marketplace name comes from the name field in that repo's marketplace.json, and codex plugin list shows it. Point it at the repo, not the raw marketplace.json URL. The command clones a git repo, so a raw file link fails with a 404. Put the plugin in ./plugins/my-plugin (repo) or ~/.codex/plugins/my-plugin (personal), then list it in .agents/plugins/marketplace.json with "source": {"source": "local", "path": "./plugins/my-plugin"}. Restart the app and it shows up. Community plugins can bundle hooks, MCP servers and shell commands. Spend two minutes on the repo: when was the last commit, what does .mcp.json start, are there hooks. Where do plugins get installed? Into ~/.codex/plugins/cache/MARKETPLACE/PLUGIN/VERSION/. Local plugins use the version local. How do I remove one? codex plugin remove plugin-name@marketplace, or uninstall from the Plugins view in the app. Why a 404 on marketplace add? Usually a raw marketplace.json URL. Give it the repo instead. The full guide, with an install command finder, is at https://pickaplugin.com/guides/install-codex-plugin

If you write code for a living, and lately you've been letting an assistant write a lot of it, it's worth knowing about. In 1978, Norman Slamecka and Peter Graf at the University of Toronto ran a set of experiments that sound almost too simple to matter. Half the time, people read a word pair in full. If you need to drop two confidential pages from a 50MB legal contract or pull three sheets out of a scanned invoice bundle, uploading the entire file to a remote server just to reorder objects wastes bandwidth and exposes sensitive documents to third-party storage. Under ISO 32000-1 (§7.7.3), a PDF stores its pages in a tree structure rooted in the document Catalog (/Root): Catalog (/Root) └── Pages Tree (/Pages) ├── Page 1 (/Page) -> Object 10 0 R ├── Page 2 (/Page) -> Object 15 0 R └── Page 3 (/Page) -> Object 20 0 R

entry.title: If you're building a DevTool or AI infrastructure company, it's time to look beyond traditional GTM.
entry.summary: There's so much more to a company than its LinkedIn profile, employee count or funding announcements. Its engineering ecosystem can tell you what it's building, what technologies it's adopting, what it's moving away from and where potential opportunities might exist. A few places worth exploring - GitHub What are they building? Which repositories are active? What frameworks and technologies are they using? Are they contributing to open source? What direction is their engineering team moving towards? Package registries Look at npm, PyPI and other package ecosystems. What are they publishing, installing, maintaining or depending on? These can reveal a lot about their actual technology choices. Docker Hub and container registries What images are they pushing? What infrastructure are they running? Are they adopting new tools or changing their existing stack? Engineering job openings What roles are they hiring for? Are they looking for Kubernetes engineers, AI infrastructure specialists, DevOps engineers or people with experience in a particular technology? Hiring often gives you a glimpse of what's coming next. Developer communities Look at Dev.to, Reddit, Stack Overflow, technical blogs and engineering discussions. What problems are they talking about? What tools are they evaluating? What are their developers experimenting with? Technology adoption and migrations Are they adopting a new technology? Moving away from an existing infrastructure? Replacing a solution? Building something internally? These movements can tell you much more than a company description ever will. The interesting part is that none of these signals, on their own, tells the complete story. But when you start connecting them, you get a much better picture of what is happening inside a company. And that's probably a much more interesting way to research an account than just looking at its LinkedIn profile. Something worth exploring if you're in technical GTM.

entry.title: Why Apple rejects apps under guideline 4.3, and a free check before you submit
entry.summary:
We had all 6 of our new App Store listings rejected under guideline 4.3 since September, while updates to our 20 live apps passed review. Here is what 4.3 says, what we learned, and the check we now run before every submission. 4.3(a): "Don't create multiple Bundle IDs of the same app." Apple's example is a separate map app for every city; it wants one app with variations through in-app purchase. 4.3(b): "Don't submit apps that are indistinguishable from what's already widely available." It names dating, flashlight, sound effects, wallpaper, simple timers and fortune telling as well-established kinds that need "a meaningfully different or improved experience." One app, not many bundle IDs. Search the store for your exact name and core idea before you submit. If you're in a named crowded category, say plainly what's different. Compare against your own catalog. Near-copies of your other apps count. Put the difference in the first lines of your description and subtitle.
Real output for the tool's built-in example listing. We automated steps 2 and 4 as a free browser tool: 4.3 Radar (https://radar43.pages.dev/). It sends your app name and three keywords to Apple's public search, compares your listing in your browser, and gives a risk level with reasons. Your description isn't sent anywhere. It covers the US store's public search and text only; it can't predict App Review. Disclosure: we built 4.3 Radar. There's an optional paid review; the check itself is free.

entry.title: サイト名がつかなくて困っているのだよ、Googleさん
entry.summary:
Decider を開発・運営しているので、その話を書いていこうと考えています。サイト名は、Decider, directly. 「Decider」で検索するとそれなりに上位に次のようなサイトが出ます。明日のことは分からないのですが、今日はこの頃は2位です。
ブランド検索については大きな問題が2点あり、ひとつはどうやってもサイト名がつかない。 結論からいうと、deciderというサイトには米国の映画メディアがありまして、そちらにはいろいろな意味で負けているのかもしれません。 「なんでDeciderなのにDeciderにならないんだ」みたいなことをずっと思ってはいましたよ。ただ、ルールもメカニズムもはっきりしたところが分からない。 どうやらグローバルで1つだと分かったときに「え、巨大サイトと争ってたの？」みたいな絵が見えてきて、その時の感想は、なんのこっちゃですよね。そちらがDeciderであるということは、うちは当然 Decider ではない。本当に？ あと余談とも言い切れない話として、カタカナのディサイダーではアイドルが活躍されております。明日のことは分からないのですが、今日はこの頃は当社はもう絶対に表示されなくなりましたよ。夏頃は出てたけどね。いまはアイドルと釣り具。 これは、ウイナー・テイクス・オールで当然ということなのでしょうか？ サイト名がフィッシングを防止するという少し違った役割を持つ点は理解するものの、法的な権利を阻害するような選択権を実効的に１社が持ってしまっている面には疑問があります。法制度が歪んでいるように見えます。 商標制度はそもそも（分野別に独占するとしても）重複は当然あることを前提とした制度であり、「ラベルは1つです」というルールを宣言することじたいが法制度と矛盾します。 しかも、日本語だったら日本しか使ってないから競合性が低いものの、英語が公用語の国はたくさんあるので、国家主権どうしが対立したら優劣の問題でもないでしょう。ここまで書いていて気づきましたが、日本国に頑張って欲しい話でもあるな。 冒頭に Decider, directly. というサイト名を書いたとおり、いま狙っているラベルはもう Decider じゃない。 たぶん、ディサイダーであれば取れるのかもしれないのですが、これだと日本から出られないサイトになってしまうので違う。 商標制度じたいは自社ブランドを識別するワードとして使用していないと権利が薄まってしまうので、使えないという制約を理解できないと同時に、使うことも課せられている。 さらに困ったことに、Decider, directly. を主張し続けているのですが、これがまた認識しない。bingにはサイト名ついたけどね。 たしかに、ドメイン文字列に一切 decider を入れてないんですよ。スターリーグのサイトだからね。ただ、ドメインで決まるとも言ってないじゃないか。 ここは確かに Decider を提供している株式会社スターリーグのドメインである star.careers だと確認したうえで Decider というラベルを付けるのが Google の仕事なわけですよ。確信が持てない、ではなくてね。確信が持てないのであれば、他のサイトにも Decider を付けたらダメという論も立つ。 いや、言いたいことは Decider から Decider のサイト名を剥奪してくれということでなくて、もはや同じラベルじゃないワードを選んで、商標権者が合理的に理解できるサイト名つけたら、暫定でもそれは付けなきゃダメなんじゃないの？ということです。 再登場させると、最近になってfaviconも表示されなくなり、もはやブランドの体裁がない状態です。継続使用による識別力の前提がありません。 いま、しつこくラベルを随所に表示するという、見ようによっては小細工を継続しており、どこかでは反映されるだろうと見ています。bingにはだいぶ前にサイト名ついたけどね。 ただ、faviconはあったものが消えたわけで、折に触れて消える程度のうたかた的存在なのかもしれないな、という見方も成立します。 要するに、Googleのサイトレベルのシグナルは、かなりバグ含みな感触を持っているのでさすがに直して欲しいと思います。

entry.summary: A thesaurus can produce a sentence with entirely new words that means something different. entry.title: Is Loop Engineering a New Technology, or Just Reheated Leftovers? Explained Through Training a Dog Classifier
entry.summary:
The Short Answer
The term "loop engineering" is everywhere right now, and it sounds like a new craft. My view: the idea is leftovers, but this is the first time the leftovers are actually edible. The leftover part: let a system iterate on its own, use a set of criteria to judge how each round went, adjust from the feedback, and repeat until the goal is met. That is the most basic machine learning training loop, and also the feedback loop from control theory. The new part: in the past, what got adjusted inside the loop had to be numbers (model parameters). Now it can be a piece of text, a file, or a knowledge base, and the feedback can be a plain sentence. That is why the pattern can, for the first time, be applied to open-ended tasks. entry.summary: vLLM and SGLang are great inference engines. If you serve chat or batch jobs, use them. But AI agents are a different workload, and I wanted to see how well these engines handle it. So I measured it. A coding agent works in turns: It sends the whole conversation to the model. The model answers with a tool call (run a command, edit a file). The agent runs the tool, appends the result, and sends the whole conversation again. In the traces I used, a median session has about 60 turns and grows to tens of thousands of tokens. Every turn re-sends everything before it. To answer a turn, the engine needs the KV cache for the full history. entry.title: Prettier on demand, on run, on save
entry.summary:
JSLab feature notes: one docs page, explained. Today: Formatting. Scratch code is written fast and formatted never. JSLab, a JavaScript & TypeScript scratchpad for macOS, formats with Prettier, so the mess you typed at speed can look like code before you paste it anywhere. ⌥⇧F (Format Code) formats the current tab. It's also in Actions → Format Code and the command palette. const order={id:42,items:[{sku:"A-1",qty:2},{sku:"B-7",qty:1}],paid:true} const total=order.items.reduce((sum,item)=>sum+item.qty,0) total
One ⌥⇧F later: const order = { id: 42, items: [ { sku: "A-1", qty: 2 }, { sku: "B-7", qty: 1 }, ], paid: true, }; const total = order.items.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.qty, 0); total;
The format lands as one undo step, and JSLab applies minimal edits instead of replacing the whole buffer, so your folds, scroll position and cursor stay where they were. Two settings, both off by default: Format on Run (Settings → General) formats before each run, unless you're typing. Format on Save (Settings → Editor) formats when you save a file. Settings → Formatting holds every Prettier option JSLab supports, with Prettier's usual defaults:
Setting Default
Print Width 80
Tab Width 2
Semicolons On
Single Quotes Off
Trailing Commas All
Arrow Parens Always
Plus Use Tabs, Quote Props, JSX Single Quotes, Bracket Spacing and Bracket Same Line. Print Width goes from 20 to 320, and Tab Width from 1 to 16. entry.title: A track record nobody can edit: SHA-256, git and Bitcoin timestamps
entry.summary:
Anyone can show an impressive track record after the fact. The question is whether the predictions existed before the outcomes. We wanted a way to prove that, cheaply, without asking anyone to trust us. Every night: The day's scores are written to a CSV file, before the next market open. The file's SHA-256 fingerprint goes into a ledger, with the publication time. The file and the ledger are committed to git and pushed to a public repository. The file is timestamped with OpenTimestamps, which anchors its hash in the Bitcoin blockchain. A ledger row looks like this: date,version,file,sha256,rows,published_at 2026-10-19,v1,scores/2026-10-19.csv,c657649932bf899f72043e60cad05f74527c9d6c22e51f7a44d57c79b2a1a560,99,2026-10-20T10:51:30+00:00
SHA-256: change a single character in the file and the fingerprint changes completely. git: history is public; rewriting it shows up for anyone who cloned earlier. OpenTimestamps: the strongest layer. The hash is committed into a Bitcoin transaction, so it proves the file existed by that block's time, and it doesn't depend on GitHub or us. It's free. One practical gotcha: git can normalise line endings on checkout, which changes the bytes and breaks the hash. A .gitattributes rule keeps the files byte-exact. sha256sum track_record/scores/2026-10-19.csv # compare with the ledger ots verify track_record/scores/2026-10-19.csv.ots
It goes into a public corrections log. The original file stays as it was. Corrections are new entries, never edits. Because "trust me" isn't evidence. With this, the scores either beat random picks over time or they don't, and nobody can quietly rewrite which. From Quantooo Lab, the makers of quantooo.com, a free, open and educational quant lab: every formula, every test and every failure is public. See it here: https://quantooo.com/track-record Educational, not investment advice.

entry.title: DMARC without breaking your own mail
entry.summary: My app sends invitation, password-reset and alert emails, and for a long time nothing seemed wrong with them. They were sent, they mostly arrived, and the DMARC record said p=none. That setting tells receivers to do nothing about mail that fails authentication, so a forged email claiming to come from my domain got delivered exactly as often as a real one. Anyone could have sent a password-reset email in my app's name with their own link in it, and my DNS would not have asked a single receiver to stop it. p=none is how you start, and it is not useless. It switches on daily reports from the receivers, and since February 2024 Gmail has required a DMARC record from anyone sending it more than 5,000 messages a day. 서론
헤드라인들은 시장 전염병, 테라/루나 붕괴, 그리고 뒤이은 쓰리애로우즈캐피탈(3AC)의 몰락에 대해 소리쳤다. 이 외부적 충격들이 셀시우스 네트워크가 파산으로 치닫게 된 주된 원인이라고 지목했지. 2022년 6월 12일, 셀시우스가 갑작스레 모든 고객의 출금, 이체, 스왑을 중단했을 때, 즉각적인 반응은 암호화폐 시장을 휩쓴 연쇄적인 실패들을 탓하는 것이었다. 하지만 이 바닥을 30년간 지켜본 사람으로서 말해주자면, 그런 외부 사건들은 분명 강력한 촉매제였지만, 셀시우스 몰락의 진짜 원인은 아니었어. 내가 보기엔 셀시우스 실패의 진짜 시작점은 훨씬 더 깊은 곳에 있었다. 그것은 리스크에 대한 근본적인 왜곡이었고, 지속 가능한 고수익이라는 환상 위에 세워진 위험천만한 사업 모델이었다. 새 시대의 블록체인 옷을 입었을 뿐, '탈중앙화'나 '투명성'의 의미를 제대로 이해하지 못한 구시대적 금융 차익거래 방식이었던 셈이다. 알렉스 마신스키의 지휘 아래, 회사는 사용자들에게 예치금에 대해 최대 17%에 달하는 수익률을 약속했다. 기관 대출자에게 자산을 빌려주고 디파이(DeFi) 전략에 참여하여 이러한 수익을 창출한다고 주장했지. 내가 보기에 문제는 단순히 무엇에 투자했느냐가 아니라, 어떻게 운영했느냐, 그리고 그 약속들의 내재된 취약성이었다. 여기서 핵심은 간단하다. 셀시우스는 갑작스럽고 예측 불가능한 시장 이벤트 때문에 무너진 게 아니라는 거다. 그것은 시한폭탄과 같았다. 시장 상황이 변하면 터지도록 설계되어 있었지. 지속 불가능한 수익 창출 모델, 심각한 자산-부채 불일치, 그리고 극심한 투명성 부족이 그…

entry.title: 整理脏数据，不要吝啬模型算力和 Token
entry.summary:
先说结论
处理一堆脏数据时，我现在更愿意先把模型能力、上下文和执行条件给足，而不是自己坐下来设计分类。尤其是大量杂乱文档的整理，真正困难的地方不是改几个标题、挪几个位置，而是要先理解所有内容，再判断它们应该怎样组织、哪些信息互相关联。 过去总觉得整理数据是简单劳动，用便宜模型就可以。实际效果不好，又以为问题在于自己没有先把结构设计清楚。现在重新想，这个判断可能一开始就错了：不是所有整理工作都适合用低成本模型做。数据越脏、越缺少明确规则，越可能需要更强的推理能力。
最近整理自己的 ChatGPT Space 资料库时，面对一大堆杂乱文档，常常不知道从哪里下手。文档多了，不只是内容需要修改，还涉及分类、归属、关联关系，以及不同资料应该如何一起维护。 我之前的想法很简单：让 AI 去做这些整理工作，应该不难，所以没有必要在模型和 Token 上花太多成本。结果整理出来的效果不理想。后来甚至开始反思，是不是应该先由自己确定整个目录架构，让 AI 按照人的分类去执行。 这个思路看起来很稳妥，却忽略了另一个可能性：如果交给 AI 的本来就是一件复杂的理解任务，我却一直用低配置的方式去做，那么问题未必出在分类方法上。 一份结构化、格式统一的数据，字段是什么意思、怎样归类、需要转换成什么样，往往都很明确。这样的工作交给脚本或者便宜模型就能处理，甚至不一定需要大模型。 但杂乱文档不是这样。它们可能来自不同时间、不同项目，表达方式不一致；有的内容是在记录过去的决定，有的是目前正在执行的规则，还有的只是一个没有展开的想法。AI 需要先判断每份材料是什么，再综合其他材料理解它的用途。 也就是说，干净数据通常是在执行规则；脏数据可能需要先发现规则、建立结构，再执行规则。后者看上去像整理杂物，实际上包含不少理解和推理。 以前恰恰在这种不确定性最高的地方节省模型能力，整理不好以后，又用自己的时间去弥补。 这次更重要的想法变化，是不再默认由人来设计分类架构。既然准备把资料库交给 AI 维护，那么目录应该怎么分、文档放在哪里、哪些内容应该关联，本来就可以是 AI 的工作。 人的输入可以很简单：这是一套什么资料，要整理到什么程度，哪些历史内容必须保留，最后希望怎样查找和使用。至于逐份阅读、提出分类、调整目录、建立链接、检查遗漏和冲突，都让 AI 去做。 我不需要一开始就看完所有文章，也不需要先替 AI 画好一张思维导图。等它整理出结果，再按需要检查结构和效果。结构仍然重要，只是设计和维护结构这件事，不必天然归人负责。 如果一个便宜模型需要反复提示、返工，最后还要人工检查大量内容，它的调用费用虽然低，整个任务未必便宜。 反过来，强模型在混乱资料的理解、归类和关系判断上，如果能够减少返工和人工介入，那么更高的 Token 成本反而可能是划算的。这里衡量的不是单次调用价格，而是从接收资料到整理完成，究竟花了多少资源和人的精力。 这也意味着模型选择应该跟着任务变化。结构稳定、规则明确以后，再把批量修改、格式转换等重复工作交给低成本模型或脚本；在最混乱、最需要判断的初始阶段，不必急着省。 当然，模型能力不是全部。即使用了最强的模型，如果只能看到一小部分文档、读不到关联资料，或者没有权限修改目录和链接，整理效果依然会受限制。 所以，我说的“把能力开到最大”，不只是切换模型，还包括让 AI 拿到完成任务所需的上下文、工具和权限。大量文档可以分批读、统一盘点，而不是受单次上下文容量限制，就误以为已经看全。 权限也不是毫无边界地允许破坏。像批量删除、覆盖原文这类可能造成损失的操作，应当有版本记录和可恢复的方式。让 AI 真正能干活，与保留必要的回滚能力并不矛盾。 这次整理资料，让我修正的不是某一套目录结构，而是评估 AI 能力的方法。 当 AI 的工作结果不理想时，过去容易马上认为：这件事还是要由人来设计、判断、处理。现在更值得先检查的是：模型是不是太弱？上下文是不是不完整？工具和权限是不是限制了它？是不是为了省 Token，反而把问题弄得更复杂？ 把资源开足不保证每次都能成功，但至少可以避免一个常见误判：拿低配置下的表现，去判断 AI 原本能做到什么程度。 尤其面对一堆脏乱、没有现成结构的资料，我更愿意先让足够强的 AI 把事情做明白。等数据整理好了，再谈怎样降低成本。

entry.title: 시뮬레이션이 예측을 넘어서려면, 분자 속으로 들어가야 한다
entry.summary:
시뮬레이션이 예측을 넘어서려면, 분자 속으로 들어가야 한다
The Generalist에 실린 심일리(Simile) 박준성 CEO 인터뷰를 읽고 밤새 잠을 설쳤다. 80억 인류 행동 85% 정확도 예측이라니—숫자만 보면 압도적이다. 하지만 개발자 관점에서 보자. 행동 로그와 클릭스트림으로 학습한 트랜스포머가 아무리 커도, 단백질이 어떻게 접히고, 효소가 어떻게 기질을 인식하며, 약물이 포켓에 어떻게 들어맞는지를 '이해'하고 있지는 않다. 가중치 공간에서의 상관관계일 뿐, 원자 단위의 인과관계는 아니다. 2년 전, 내 팀은 알파폴드2(AlphaFold 2) 예측 구조로 타겟 단백질의 바인딩 포켓을 스크리닝하다가 벽에 부딪혔다. 정전기 표면도, 수소결합 네트워크, 입체 장애—이 모든 게 2D 뷰포트 위에서는 평평하게 납작해진다. PyMOL에서 돌리다가, ChimeraX에서 회전시키다가, 결국 OpenMM으로 200 ns 분자동역학을 돌려 앙상블을 뽑아내니 비로소 유연한 루프가 열리는 순간을 포착할 수 있었다. GPU 클러스터에서 8×A100으로 병렬 프리페어링을 걸고, MM‑PBSA로 자유에너지를 재계산하니 hit‑rate이 3 %에서 12 %로 뛰었다. 그 경험이 말해준다. 정적 구조만으로는 ‘결합 가능하다’는 가설만 남고, 동적 앙상블과 양자‑역학 보정이 있어야 비로소 ‘결합한다’는 확신을 얻는다. 지금도 밤마다 트레이닝 로그를 보며, 다음 스텝에서 어떤 컨포머가 등장할지 상상한다. 자세한 내용은 Simile 공식 사이트에서 확인해 보세요.

I use both to estimate property tax bills, so a wrong rate turns directly into a wrong number on a page. The 2025 county file says Fort Bend County's rate is $0.824 per $100 of taxable value. The rate the county actually adopted is $0.412. On a home with $300,000 of taxable value, that is a $1,236 difference in the county line of the bill. The file is labeled "Working" and dated 01/28/2026, so this isn't a complaint about the Comptroller. It's a report built from what thousands of local units submit. But it is the kind of error a data pipeline will happily carry through, and the interesting part is which checks catch it. A Texas county rate has three…

entry.title: Godot UI with AI: a main menu and settings screen that don't clip (tested)
entry.summary: Can an AI build Godot UI that holds together when the window changes size? We asked Ziva, an AI agent that runs inside the Godot editor, for a main menu and a settings screen made of Control nodes. In 3 minutes 58 seconds it built both scenes, ran the game, clicked Settings and Back, and checked the layout at five window sizes. Nothing was clipped. It also missed something: the Fullscreen checkbox was nearly invisible when unchecked, and Ziva reported "all controls showing". A second prompt asking it to look closely caught and fixed it. Layout is where people say AI help breaks down. entry.title: Claude Code Game Studios: Desenvolvimento de Jogos com IA
entry.summary:
O que é
O Claude Code Game Studios é um sistema que transforma o Claude Code em um estúdio de desenvolvimento de jogos, utilizando 49 agentes de IA e 72 habilidades de fluxo de trabalho. O processo inicia com a descrição de um jogo; a ferramenta faz perguntas para definir a mecânica e a estética, cria um brief de design e constrói um protótipo jogável no navegador. O sistema inclui verificações automáticas para garantir que o jogo abra sem erros e que as funcionalidades do brief foram implementadas. É voltado para desenvolvedores ou entusiastas que desejam criar jogos de forma iterativa. O sistema serve para quem quer transformar ideias simples em projetos reais, permitindo adicionar funcionalidades passo a passo, criar painéis de ajuste com controles deslizantes para valores do jogo e, eventualmente, converter o protótipo em um projeto web profissional com Vite e TypeScript. Também é útil para quem já possui um jogo e deseja importá-lo para aprimorá-lo. Primeiro, instale os pré-requisitos: Git, Claude Code (via instalador nativo ou npm), Python 3 e Bash. Para testar e validar os jogos, é necessário ter o Chrome, Edge ou Chromium. Para transformar o protótipo em um projeto web completo, o Node.js é recomendado. Após a configuração, clone o repositório, abra o Claude Code e utilize o comando /prototype seguido da descrição da ideia do seu jogo para iniciar o desenvolvimento. git clone https://github.com/Donchitos/Claude-Code-Game-Studios.git my-game cd my-game
🔗 Repositório oficial: https://github.com/Donchitos/Claude-Code-Game-Studios
📚 Mais conteúdos do canal: https://gist.github.com/VictorHugodaSilvaSousa/d1e955e97cd27fc662351821d0a3fdbe

entry.title: Reading Brazil's credit card revolving rate from the central bank API (no key needed)
entry.summary:
Brazil's central bank (Banco Central do Brasil) publishes the average revolving credit card rate for individuals as series 25477 in its SGS time-series service. The API is public, needs no key and returns JSON. curl -s "https://api.bcb.gov.br/dados/serie/bcdata.sgs.25477/dados?formato=json&dataInicial=01/09/2025&dataFinal=30/09/2026"
Each row looks like {"data":"01/09/2026","valor":"15.29"}. The value is the monthly rate in percent, as a string, and the date is always day 01 of the month. September 2026: 15.29% per month. September 2025: 15.23% per month. The monthly rate stayed between 14.90% (Jan 2026) and 15.44% (May 2025) over the last 24 months. The API gives monthly only. The yearly rate is (1 + m)^12 - 1: m = 0.1529 print(round(((1 + m) ** 12 - 1) * 100, 2)) # 451.44
R$ 1,000 left untouched for 12 months at that rate becomes about R$ 5,514 (1000 * 1.1529 ** 12). In Brazil, Law 14.690/2023 caps interest and fees at 100% of the original debt, so the real ceiling is double. valor is a string with a dot, not a comma. Date params use dd/mm/aaaa, not ISO. The series is the average reported by institutions, not the rate on your card. I put the full 24-month table and the method on a page (in Portuguese), with sentences ready to cite: https://tobbofin.com/calculadoras/juros-do-cartao-banco-central/. I work on Tobbo, a personal finance app for Android that connects to Brazilian banks through Open Finance. The page is ours. Source: Banco Central do Brasil, SGS series 25477, checked on 2026-11-09.

Stockfish can tell you that 17...Bh6 dropped your win chance from 72% to 31%. What it won't tell you is the part that actually makes you better: You were trying to create a kingside attack. Quando a auditoria interna de IA vira teatro de calendário
O número que a norma não dá
Não existe um número de auditorias por ano escrito na ISO 42001. Sou auditor de sistemas críticos, e essa é a primeira coisa que preciso desfazer quando alguém me pergunta de quanto em quanto tempo deve auditar os próprios sistemas de IA. A cláusula 9.2 pede três coisas: intervalos planejados, imparcialidade de quem audita e evidência documentada do que foi verificado. Ela não separa sistema de alto risco de sistema trivial.
