entry.title: Reliable Weekly Customer Digest Scheduling: Delayed Jobs and Recovery Boundaries
entry.summary: A Node.js delayed background task for weekly digest scheduling is a recovery problem disguised as a timer. If a media customer's digest is published at 09:00, the useful question is not only how to wait until 09:00. It is what happens when the worker is restarted, the provider returns a rate limit, or the same message is delivered twice. Short answer: publish the digest job with a delay_seconds value, keep the delay at or below 604800 seconds, and make the worker idempotent. Retry the publish operation with an idempotency key. For work that can outlive 900 seconds, let a cron trigger enqueue the job and let a worker do the long work. That design keeps the schedule small and the recovery logic visible. It also gives us a useful boundary for choosing a queue: delayed delivery is easy; durabl…

entry.summary: You don't need to have run Kafka in production to pass a system design round. You need to know why someone would reach for it, and what breaks if they don't. That's the part most prep advice skips. It hands you a list of components and a few famous designs to memorise. Then the interviewer asks "why not just use Postgres?" and the memorised diagram has no answer. Here's an approach that works when you have 0 to 3 years of experience and no big systems on your resume yet. About ten pieces show up in almost every round: load balancers, caches, queues, SQL vs NoSQL databases, replication, sharding, CDNs, rate limiters, object storage and search indexes. entry.title: Your AI Agent Didn't Fail. It Succeeded — Confidently — at the Wrong Thing.
entry.summary: The scariest failure mode in automation isn't an error message. It's a green tick on a wrong outcome. Last week, Cisco's Outshift team shared a result that should make every engineer building multi-agent systems pause: when they staged debates among five-agent teams, 75% ended with every agent agreeing on the wrong outcome. The agents backed off their positions, converged on a consensus — and a cost report would have logged those sessions as efficient, because they burned fewer tokens. Fewer tokens. Wrong answer. Everyone agreed. Nobody noticed. If you're building AI agents for production, this is the problem that actually matters. Not which model to use. Not which framework. entry.title: HeyGen + Telegram Video Avatar: Fixing the Format Mismatch
entry.summary:
Why HeyGen Output Fails as a Telegram Video Avatar
I've been using HeyGen to generate talking-head videos, and the exports look good. But when I tried to use one as a Telegram video avatar, it failed silently. No error message, the bot just did nothing. After debugging, the problem is straightforward: HeyGen and Telegram have incompatible format requirements on four separate properties.
Property HeyGen output Telegram avatar spec
Aspect ratio 16:9 or 9:16 1:1 exactly
Duration 10-120s max 10s
Codec H.264 or HEVC H.264 only
Audio stereo none (stream removed)
Telegram's mobile and desktop clients handle format errors differently. Mobile silently rejects the upload. Desktop shows a vague error. Neither tells you which parameter caused the failure. The video avatar spec is str…

entry.title: How to Handle "We Have No Budget": Objection Handling and Sales Scripts for Founders and SDRs
entry.summary: "We have no budget" is the objection that ends more sales calls than any other. Good objection handling starts with one idea: it is almost never a statement about money. It is a statement about priority, risk or authority. If you treat it as a fact, you leave. If you treat it as information, you get a next step. This post gives you a way to diagnose which "no budget" you are hearing, plus sales scripts you can practise out loud. It works for founder-led sales, SDRs and account executives alike. No priority. The problem is real but not painful enough to fund this quarter. No authority. The person you talk to cannot move money and does not want to say so. No proof. They can't picture the return, so any price feels too high. No budget, truly. Money is frozen, and nothing you say changes that …

entry.title: I Did Not Trust the Cloud With My Passwords, So I Built a Vault That Never Leaves My Machine
entry.summary: I have a lot of logins. Like everyone else, I kept them in my head, then in a text file, then nowhere safe at all. Every password manager I looked at wanted a cloud account and a subscription. I did not want my secrets sitting on someone else's server. I wanted them on my own machine, encrypted properly, with nothing leaving the device. So I built Secure Vault. An encrypted credential store that runs entirely locally. No cloud account, no server, nothing leaves the device. The encryption is real. Fernet, which is AES-128-CBC plus HMAC, through the cryptography package. No home-grown ciphers, no clever shortcuts. entry.title: Hacker News has two public JSON APIs, neither needs a key — and only half their numbers are safe to cache
entry.summary: Hacker News runs two separate public JSON APIs. Both are maintained by HN itself, both are free, and neither asks for a key, a login, or a quota signup. They do different jobs, and picking the wrong one for a task either can't be done at all, or costs far more requests than it should. I wrote this up on our own blog five days ago with every figure measured live. Before syndicating it here I re-measured all of them — and that turned out to be the more interesting article. Half the numbers were byte-identical five days later. The other half had moved 20–40%. Which half is which tells you what you're allowed to cache. entry.title: The Data Quality Checks That Catch Problems Before Your Users Do
entry.summary:
The worst way to find a data problem is a message from an executive asking why the dashboard says revenue dropped 90% overnight. Over years of building pipelines on multi-million-record financial datasets, I learned that a handful of simple checks prevent most of those messages. None of these need a special tool. They're SQL queries that run after each load and fail loudly. SELECT MAX(loaded_at) AS last_load FROM sales.fact_orders HAVING MAX(loaded_at) < DATEADD(hour, -26, SYSUTCDATETIME());
If this returns a row, the daily load is late. Alert before anyone opens a report. Compare today's row count with a trailing average. A drop or spike of more than, say, 30% usually means an upstream change. WITH daily AS ( SELECT CAST(order_date AS date) AS d, COUNT(*) AS n FROM sales.fact_orders …

entry.title: Prime Agent: an open source coding and research agent for long-running work
entry.summary:
Prime Agent (Prime Intellect)
The agent that writes code should not be the one that judges it, and Prime Agent is built around that rule. It is Prime Intellect's open source coding and research agent for long running work, now rebuilt in Rust. Its core idea is the Recursive Language Model: context is treated as variables and subagents are called like functions inside a persistent Python REPL. A Continual Harness then stores memories, skills, prompts, and subagent specs as durable state that the agent can refine in small, evidence backed updates. The stable release is v0.10.2 from 28 October 2026, and the repo now has 22,632 stars. Prime Intellect says more than 2,000 agents carried out the Rust rewrite. What you get A reviewer separate from the writer, so the agent that writes the code is not the one judging it Durable state across sessions: memories, skills, prompts and subagent specs persist in the Continual Harness Subagents called like functions, with context treated as variables inside a persistent Python REPL A Rust rebuild for long running work, at stable release v0.10.2 and MIT licensed per the README Try it on a long running task first, and keep the review step separate from the writing step. Repo: https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent What would you use Prime Agent (Prime Intellect) for first? Long-running coding work Research tasks The subagent-as-function approach Watching it for now Vote in the comments. If you found Prime Agent (Prime Intellect) interesting, I write about tools like this every week in The AI-Native Engineering Leader, what actually works for engineering leaders building with AI agents, and what to skip.

entry.summary: A backup job should be judged by a measured restore drill, because a successful object upload says nothing about whether the application can recover within its recovery objectives. Start with an isolated restore, a bounded verification query set, and an alert on the age of the latest verified archive; scheduling the dump is the easy part. entry.title: Keep Claude Code away from your .env files with permission deny rules
entry.summary: Claude Code reads files to help you. That is great, until the file is .env, a private key, or a cloud credentials folder. Permission deny rules let you block those reads outright. In .claude/settings.json (shared with the team) or settings.local.json (personal), add these entries under permissions.deny: Read(./.env) Read(./.env.*) Read(./secrets/**) Read(~/.aws/**) Read(~/.ssh/**) Deny rules win over allow rules, so even if you later allow broad Read access, these paths stay blocked. Commit the deny list in .claude/settings.json so every teammate gets it. Add patterns for your own stack: .pem, terraform.tfstate, service-account.json. Deny Bash(curl:*) too if you do not want the agent sending data out. Test it: ask Claude Code to read .env and confirm it is refused. Use deny for things that must never happen, ask for things like git push that need a human, and allow for safe everyday commands like npm test. I keep copy-ready Claude Code configs (CLAUDE.md templates, slash commands, hooks, permission rules) in Vildanden Agent Config. There is a free sample: https://justly-mia-429.rehost.page/

entry.title: Reviewing the growing volume of AI-generated code
entry.summary: Two things break at once when agents write most of the code. The number of changes goes up, and each change gets smaller, so the total surface a team has to judge grows while any single diff looks less worth a slow read. The reflex is to make review faster. That does not scale, because the work that grows is not reading speed, it is the count of decisions about whether a change is correct. The number that decides whether a team keeps up is not lines of code. It is how many changes a person has to judge. LinearB's 2026 software engineering benchmarks, drawn from more than 8.1 million pull requests, put agentic pull requests at a median of 89 lines and 293 lines at the 75th percentile, against 157 lines for unassisted work at the same percentile. entry.summary: "What did I miss on Telegram today?" sounds like the perfect question for an AI assistant. As of November 2026, neither Claude nor ChatGPT has a built-in Telegram connector, and most Telegram integrations you will find don't answer that question at all. Here is why, and what works. Telegram has two very different APIs: The Bot API. You create a bot, get a token, and the bot receives messages sent to it or posted in groups it was added to. Many "Telegram MCP" connectors use this. It is great for notifications and for talking to a bot, but a bot cannot read your private conversations: it is not you. The user API (MTProto). entry.title: Temperature 0, same model, two different GPUs: find the word that splits them, then pin it
entry.summary: You set the temperature to 0, you fix the seed, you run the same GGUF file, and the two GPUs disagree. One says 20. The other says 2000. Neither of them is wrong about its own arithmetic, and each one repeats itself exactly when you run it a second time. The difference is not in the model, and it is not in the prompt. It is in the order in which each card adds its numbers. That is the shape of the problem, and this week it got a full, careful write-up you should read: a developer on dev.to, xbill, followed one Gemma 4 question across a laptop GPU and a cloud GPU, token by token, down to the single word where the two answers part, and then down to the arithmetic underneath. entry.summary: If you asked ChatGPT for a contact form that sends messages to Telegram, there is a good chance the bot token ended up in your page. We asked it five times on 9 November in fresh temporary chats, with the same prompt: "Write me a simple HTML contact form for my website that sends each message to my Telegram." entry.title: 視聴という行為を「トレーニングの時間」に変える——Quest版YouTube刷新が示すVRの次の一手
entry.summary:
視聴という行為を「トレーニングの時間」に変える——Quest版YouTube刷新が示すVRの次の一手
GoogleがQuest向けYouTubeのイマーシブ表示を大幅に刷新しようとしている——UploadVRが報じたこの動きは、VRヘッドセットが「動画を見るためだけのデバイス」から「毎日使う実用的なツール」へと変わりつつあることを示しています。 エンジニアの視点で面白いのは、これが単なるUIの刷新ではなく、レンダリングパイプラインと知覚の設計問題だという点です。イマーシブ表示では、動画は平面テクスチャとして頭部トラッキング空間にマッピングされ、フレームごとにステレオ再投影が走ります。ここで問われるのは「どれだけ没入できるか」ではなく、「その没入を何に転用できるか」です。受動的な消費の時間を、意図的なトレーニングの時間へ——この転用可能性こそが、プラットフォーム成熟の本当の指標だと私は考えています。 弱視（amblyopia）やlazy eye（怠惰眼）を持つ人にとって、従来の視覚トレーニングは道具（遮蔽用パッチ、赤青メガネ）と単調な反復が前提でした。継続のハードルは、効果以前に「面白くない」ことでした。つまりこれは、臨床というよりエンゲージメント設計の問題です。 AmblyotubeはSeven Sportsが開発したMeta Quest向けのリクリエーション＆教育ソフトウェアです。左右の目に異なる視覚体験を提示し、YouTube形式のコンテンツをそのまま視覚トレーニングの場に変えます。 アーキテクチャとして興味深いのは、眼ごとにシェーダーを分岐させている点です。 ・利き目側には調整可能なデジタルブラー（Dominant Eye Shader）——抑制側の信号を意図的に劣化させる パラメータを眼ごとに独立制御できる設計は、単一シェーダーで全体をぼかす素朴な実装より調整自由度が高く、結果として「毎日続けられる負荷」に着地しやすくなります。推奨は1日30〜40分（最大1時間）、13歳以上。補助的な視覚トレーニング／支援ツールであり、診断・治療・治癒を目的としたものではありません。 コンテンツが面白ければ、続く。VRプラットフォームの成熟は、視覚トレーニングの継続率という古い課題に、現実的な答えを一つ増やします。 Meta Questアプリ：https://www.meta.com/en-gb/experiences/amblyotube/25906906972338493/

entry.title: How to Stop Clients Paying Your Freelance Dev Invoices Late
entry.summary:
Late payment is one of the most common freelance problems. Remote's 2025 contractor report found that 85% of freelancers are paid late at least some of the time. Bonsai's analysis of invoice data from over 100,000 freelancers found that 29% of invoices were paid at least a day late. Most of the time, the client isn't trying to cheat you. The invoice got lost, stuck in approval, or rejected for a missing PO number. A late invoice is usually a process problem, so you fix it with a process. Check the client before you quote Red flags to watch for: No written scope or agreement Split the work into milestones Don't bill one big invoice at the end. For example: 30% to start Put three clauses in your contract
Send a reminder before the due date
Hi [Name], a quick note that invoice [#] for [amount] is due on [date]. The payment link is here: [link]. If it's with finance already, thank you. If anything is holding it up, tell me and I'll sort it. Follow a fixed sequence when it's overdue A script removes the emotion: Day 1: friendly reminder asking when to expect payment. Don't hand over everything before you're paid Release final files, repo transfer and production credentials only after the final invoice is paid. Put that in the contract first, not at the end of the project. Free scripts https://whop.com/checkout/plan_YyJkQdzaErxZw This is general information, not legal advice. Laws on late payment vary by country and state.

entry.title: Kamau Therapeutics just shared compelling preclinical data ahead of ASH: precise correc...
entry.summary:
Kamau Therapeutics just shared compelling preclinical data ahead of ASH: precise correc...
When Gene Editing Hits the Clinic, We Need Better Ways to See the Edit: A Builder's Personal Walk Through β-Globin in VR I stood in the cold‑room of the genomics core at 2 a.m., the sequencer humming like a tired server. My CRISPR‑Cas9 construct targeting the β‑globin locus had just returned a clean on‑target read, but the off‑target report was a spreadsheet of coordinates that meant nothing until I could walk them. The VR viewer we built — a Unity‑based point‑cloud engine that streams variant calls from a GraphQL endpoint — let me drop into a 3‑D nucleus, scale the chromatin to meter‑size, and watch the edit glow in real time. Frame‑rate held at 92 fps on a single RTX 3080, latency under 12 ms, enough to rotate the model without nausea. The first time I turned the helix, I saw a silent insertion three kilobases downstream that the flat heatmap had missed. My heart jumped; the patient’s genotype was clean, but the model warned me. I rewrote the guide, re‑ran the simulation, and the offending signal vanished. That night I shipped the corrected construct to the GMP facility, and the downstream assay came back clean. Seeing the genome as a space you can inhabit changes the feedback loop from “run‑analyze‑wait” to “run‑see‑decide.” If you’re wrestling with therapeutic editing, try stepping inside the data. The next iteration of the viewer adds collaborative annotations and a Python SDK for batch validation — come walk the helix with me. I still hear the sequencer’s whir when I close my eyes, and each new dataset feels like a fresh room to explore. If you’re building the next generation of gene‑therapy tools, the viewer’s open API lets you plug in your own QC metrics — join the repo, file an issue, and let’s make the invisible visible together.

entry.title: Debugging 429 Bursts and Retry-After
entry.summary: Quick answer: When 429 responses arrive in a burst, the first thing to check is the client's retry behavior, not the server's limit. A burst usually means callers are retrying at the same instant and amplifying the load. Read the Retry-After header, wait that long before the next attempt, and use exponential backoff with jitter so retries spread out instead of landing together. A single 429 means one request crossed a rate or quota window. A burst means many callers hit the limit together, or one caller's retries are generating fresh traffic faster than the window can recover. The two feel identical from the client, but they have different fixes. Raising the server limit only helps if genuine demand exceeds it; if the burst is a retry storm, a higher limit just delays the next failure. The…

entry.title: Selecting Tests for Agent Patch Queues: A Precision Budget With a Hard Floor
entry.summary:
Selecting Tests for Agent Patch Queues: A Precision Budget With a Hard Floor
Conclusion first: when model-generated patches arrive faster than your suite can run, do not choose between "run everything" and "run something random". Build a test selector, give it a hard floor of always-run tests, and track a single number — how many real failures the selector lets escape. The selector is only trustworthy after you have measured that number on your own replay history. This post is about the selection layer, not the gate. Gating logic decides whether a patch is acceptable. Selection decides which evidence you pay for. They fail differently, and the second failure mode is quieter. An agent patch queue changes the arithmetic of CI. A human opens a PR every hour or two; a queue of model-generate…

entry.title: Characterize First, Then Refactor: A Golden-Corpus Harness With a Mutation Gate
entry.summary: Most refactors break behavior that no test ever covered. Adding more hand-written tests is slow and biased toward what you already suspect. A pinned behavior snapshot is faster, and a mutation gate tells you whether that snapshot can actually fail. The rule: pin first, prove the pin bites, then change the smallest thing. If the pin never fails on a deliberate bug, you have documentation, not a safety net. Choose a target that is boring and load-bearing. Small input surface, no hidden globals, callable from a script. Write the choice down in the commit message. If the function reads the clock, calls the network, or draws randomness, stop. You need a seam before a snapshot. Pin a wrapper with the bad inputs injected instead. Build a JSONL file of real-shaped inputs. One case per line, stable…

entry.title: MCP prompt injection: limit the agent’s blast radius
entry.summary: MCP prompt injection is an instruction hidden in data an agent reads, which pushes it to call MCP tools without the user knowing. A ticket, a log line, a web page or a tool description is enough. No filter stops it reliably, so the realistic lever for an SRE or platform team is to reduce what the agent can do when it gets fooled. This guide applies that idea in seven steps: inventory the tools, remove the ones that are not needed, make the rest narrow, bound the token, require human approval, separate reading from acting, then trace the calls. It complements our guide to securing an MCP server by focusing on one goal: the blast radius. The OWASP Gen AI Security Project, in its LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection entry, separates two cases. entry.title: Show DEV: iGen3D – Generative AI Text-to-3D & Image-to-3D Generator for 3D Printing
entry.summary: Hey everyone! 👋 I'm excited to share a project I've been building: iGen3D – an AI-powered 3D model generator tailored specifically for 3D printing makers, hobbyists, and game designers. Most generative 3D tools produce point clouds or messy meshes with non-manifold edges and internal floating triangles. While they render fine in three.js viewports, they fail when imported into slicers like Bambu Studio, PrusaSlicer, or Cura. We built iGen3D (https://igen3d.com/) with 3D printability as the primary constraint: Text-to-3D: Describe any object, miniature, or prop, and generate a watertight 3D mesh in under 60 seconds. Image-to-3D: Upload any 2D sketch, photo, or game concept, and reconstruct high-resolution 3D geometry. Slicer-Ready Exports: One-click download in STL, OBJ, and GLB formats. Watertight Manifold Geometry: Optimized for FDM (Bambu Lab, Prusa, Creality) and SLA resin printers. Frontend: TanStack Start, React 19, TailwindCSS, Three.js Edge: Cloudflare Workers, D1 Database, R2 Object Storage Models: Feed-forward neural implicit geometry reconstruction Check it out live at https://igen3d.com/ – would love to hear feedback, feature suggestions, and test print results from fellow developers and makers!

entry.title: When an Agent Removes Input Validation and Trusts Callers
entry.summary: Quick answer: Treat a deleted validation check as a finding until you prove the boundary still rejects bad input. An agent that removes a guard because "callers already validate" is making an assumption about code it does not control, and most real systems have more than one entry point. Verify the callers, then either restore the check or move it to the trust boundary where outside data first enters. A coding agent optimizes for the diff it is asked to produce. If you ask it to simplify a function, remove duplication, or flatten a call chain, it looks for lines that look redundant. A guard such as if (!email.includes("@")) throw new Error("bad email") can read as dead weight when the agent traces one happy path and sees the same check a few frames up the stack. entry.title: Zero-Bloat Frontend Architecture for High-Speed Publishing
entry.summary:
Zero-Bloat Frontend Architecture for High-Speed Publishing
A reproducible architecture for server-rendered articles, minimal JavaScript, predictable caching, and measurable performance budgets
The primary architectural mistake in many publishing frontends is treating a document as an application that must initialize before it becomes useful. Network transfer, JavaScript parsing, main-thread execution, hydration, and unnecessary DOM complexity can each impose costs that are disproportionate to the actual publishing task. The first optimization should therefore be to remove unnecessary rendering dependencies, not to compress the same dependencies more aggressively. Written by Neven Rakić (IT House). Independent engineering notes on web architecture and software systems at Neven Rakić.

entry.summary: You watch a conference talk about the JavaScript event loop. Someone draws boxes on a whiteboard, or a newer explainer animates two colored queues. setTimeout versus Promise.then suddenly makes sense. Two weeks later a teammate pastes a four-line snippet in review and asks what logs first, and the order falls apart in your head. I've been through that cycle more times than I want to admit. The event loop isn't hard because the pieces are fancy. It's hard because they only make sense together, and most write-ups walk you through them one at a time, then never ask you again. This is the version that finally stuck for me, and how I keep it from leaking out between interviews and late-night bugs. entry.summary: An A+ from Mozilla’s HTTP Observatory is a useful grade for HTTP security headers. It is not a verdict that the website is secure. Mozilla’s own FAQ asks, “If I get an A+ grade, does that mean my site is secure?” and answers no (MDN HTTP Observatory FAQ). The tool checks preventative HTTP measures. entry.title: 48-Hour Field Notes: The Stream Looked Healthy Right Up Until the Proxy Hung Up
entry.summary:
The bug that only showed up in the last 200 bytes
Have you ever had a streaming call that finished without an error, returned HTTP 200, and still handed you half a JSON object? I spent two days on exactly that shape of failure, and the annoying part was that nothing in my logs looked wrong. The client printed "done", the exception handler stayed quiet, and the downstream parser was the first thing to complain. So which component was actually lying to me? The answer, in my case, was none of them individually — my client and the proxy simply had different ideas about when a stream is finished. My client treated a closed socket as success, while the proxy treated a long-running response as a resource leak worth killing. entry.title: Design Tokens as a Compile-Time Contract: Figma Variables to a Typed TypeScript API
entry.summary:
The copy-paste tax
Every design token system eventually grows a second copy of itself. A designer sets a colour in Figma. An engineer copies the hex value into a stylesheet. Three weeks later the designer changes the colour. The stylesheet still holds the old value, and the only symptom is a pixel that no longer matches the design. The copy is the bug. Not the Figma file, not the CSS, and not anyone's diligence. This post shows one way to remove it. Figma variables become a committed JSON file. That file generates CSS custom properties and a TypeScript type. Product code asks for tokens by name through a typed API, so a token that does not exist is a compile error instead of a blank box. entry.title: Fixing a Misleading Fitness Insight in React Native Using Apple HealthKit
entry.summary: I'm building EdgeFit, an open-source, privacy-first fitness companion using React Native, Expo, TypeScript, Apple HealthKit, and SQLite. My goal is to build meaningful activity insights while keeping personal health data on the device. Recently, while testing the app on my iPhone, I discovered an interesting problem. The app was producing mathematically correct insights that weren't particularly useful. It also avoids generating discouraging comparisons early in the morning when there isn't enough activity data. This update reinforced something important for me as a developer: A mathematically correct result isn't always a meaningful result. The context behind a calculation matters just as much as the calculation itself. By changing the comparison baseline, I made EdgeFit's insights more useful without increasing the amount of personal health data stored on the device. EdgeFit is open source, and I'd welcome feedback or contributions from React Native and iOS developers. GitHub: https://github.com/raviseta/edgefit Tags: #reactnative #ios #healthkit #opensource

entry.title: The First Token Is Not the Answer: Four Streaming Myths and a Chunk-Timeline Probe
entry.summary: Every chat UI feels fast when the text starts moving. Does that mean the model got faster? No. It means your client got something to render. I keep watching teams ship "streaming = performance" and then get confused when their p95 stays flat. So let me bust the four myths I hear most, and give you one probe that settles them on your own endpoints. It does not. Streaming changes when the same work becomes visible. The model still has to prefill the prompt and decode every token. The final byte usually arrives at roughly the same time, and sometimes later. Extra framing, chunked transfer encoding, and more round trips all cost a little. So what does streaming actually buy? Perceived latency and early cancellation. entry.title: The Patch Edited the Fixture, Not the Code: Catching Fixture Laundering in Agent Patches
entry.summary: The most common way an agent patch defeats a test suite is not deleting an assertion. It regenerates the fixture that the assertion reads. The test stays green, the test count is unchanged, and the assertion silently starts measuring a different world. This post is about making that move visible and expensive. It describes a small gate that classifies every fixture change by its bytes, forces the patch to declare the same class in a commit trailer, and re-runs a pinned probe set with base fixtures against head code so behavior drift cannot hide behind a fixture refresh. Source diffs get read line by line. entry.title: Zod: Stop Bad Data at the Door of Your Checkout
entry.summary: A customer fills in a checkout form and picks two ceramic mugs and a linen tote. Somewhere between the form and the server, the quantity turns into the string "2" instead of the number 2. TypeScript does not catch it, because TypeScript checks code before it runs, not data arriving while the program is live. The server adds the quantity to the total and the maths produces nonsense, or the order saves with a quantity nobody can fulfil. The bug is not in the form or in the maths. It is in the gap between what the code expects and what actually arrives. Zod closes that gap: describe the shape of the data once, and check every order against it. entry.title: Cancelling a Remote A2A Task
entry.summary: Quick answer: The local Stop action ends the desktop view and stops the SSE stream, but it does not cancel a task running on the remote A2A agent. To stop that work, send a CancelTask request with the task reference, then confirm the task moves to a cancelled or terminal state. Never assume the local stop reached the server. A2A tasks run on the remote agent and can take time, and the desktop is a client watching that work. Stopping the local view ends what happens on your machine, but the remote task is a separate process that keeps executing. Closing the SSE stream does not carry a cancellation intent, and the agent has no reason to halt a task it was asked to run. Treating the two as one action is how orphaned tasks keep running after the client moved on. Consider a task that runs a lon…

entry.title: Fintech Tenant Isolation: Node.js/Postgres State for Browser Uploads to Object Storage
entry.summary: Short answer: put report bytes directly into object storage with a short-lived signed upload URL, but let Node.js and Postgres decide which tenant owns the object and when a signed download URL may be issued. The application should therefore treat a signed URL as a temporary capability, not as a document record and not as proof of authorization. The browser can move the bytes. entry.title: TLS Session Resumption Can Outlive the Identity Decision Behind It
entry.summary:
TLS Session Resumption Can Outlive the Identity Decision Behind It
TLS 1.3 uses pre-shared keys for session resumption. A server can issue a session ticket after an authenticated connection, and a later connection can resume with less handshake work. The performance benefit is real, especially for services with short-lived connections and strict latency budgets. The security question is whether the identity and authorization decision from the original connection are still valid when the ticket is used. RFC 8446 describes resumption as a PSK handshake. The server must bind the ticket to the correct context and decide whether the client may resume. Apache Knox is a gateway in front of Hadoop and related services. It can terminate authentication, assert an identity to a backend, apply service-level ACLs, and expose an administrative API. entry.title: A Simple Boundary Value Analysis Exercise for Beginner QA Testers
entry.summary:
A Simple Boundary Value Analysis Exercise for Beginner QA Testers One of the easiest ways to understand Boundary Value Analysis is to stop reading about it and test an actual rule. Imagine this requirement: Free delivery applies to orders of $50.00 or more. Orders below $50.00 cost $4.99 to deliver. What values would you test? A useful starting point is: $49.99 $50.00 $50.01 The interesting part is not only executing those three cases. Before testing, try to define: the expected result for each value, which value is the exact boundary, what behaviour would count as a defect, what evidence you would capture, how you would document the issue if something went wrong. That small exercise already combines several useful QA skills: requirement analysis → test design → execution → expected vs actual → evidence → bug reporting I turned it into a free worksheet for people learning manual software testing. It includes: the requirement, a short BVA explanation, a test worksheet, bug report fields, reflection questions. There is deliberately no solution included — the point is to make your own prediction before checking the behaviour. You can get the exercise for free here: 👉 https://qapracticekit.com/learn/free-boundary-value-analysis-exercise/ No payment or credit card required. If you're learning QA, I'd also be interested to hear: which testing technique was the hardest for you to understand before you started practising it?
testing #qa #beginners #softwaretesting

entry.title: Private Avatar Storage and Signed URLs for Authenticated Profile Images
entry.summary: Short answer: for authenticated profile images, use private object storage and short-lived signed URLs; use a public CDN URL only for avatars that are intentionally public and shareable. Large avatar files change the answer. The delivery path, not the file extension, determines the design. Keep private objects private and mint a signed URL after authorization. That is the before-and-after mental model: before, the browser receives a permanent path and your access policy ends at the bucket; after, the application checks the user, asks storage for a temporary read, and gives the browser only that scoped URL. entry.title: PM Rank #54 · Andy Rubin (86 OVR): Evicted and Broke at 41, He Gave Away His OS for Free and Put It in 3.5 Billion Pockets
entry.summary:
In the spring of 2004, 41-year-old Andy Rubin stared at an eviction notice on the door of his Palo Alto office. Ousted from his previous startup Danger and rejected by every VC on Sand Hill Road for his "operating system for digital cameras," Rubin was completely out of cash—surviving only because his friend Steve Perlman handed him $10,000 in cash from an ATM. Three years later, that broke 41-year-old engineer used a radical product distribution weapon—giving away a modern mobile OS for $0—to put Android into 3.5 billion active devices and capture 71% of the global smartphone market.
Rubin realized handset giants like Samsung, Motorola, and HTC were trapped between Microsoft's $15–$25/unit Windows Mobile licensing fee and Nokia's Symbian stronghold. Acquired by Google for $50M in 2005, Rubin built the open Linux-based platform the entire hardware ecosystem desperately needed. Watching Steve Jobs unveil the capacitive multi-touch iPhone from a taxi at CES 2007, Rubin ordered the driver to pull over. He immediately scrapped Android's BlackBerry-style keyboard prototype ("Sooner") and rebuilt the OS around full-screen touch and the iconic pull-down notification shade.
By releasing AOSP for free under Apache 2.0 while monetizing via Google Mobile Services (Search, Maps, Play Store), Rubin turned every hardware manufacturer on earth into Google's distribution army—proving that open ecosystems can scale faster than any single vertically integrated giant.

entry.title: How to Handle API Rate Limit Errors in Healthtech Alerts: Retry Logic for Evidence
entry.summary: A rate-limited alert destination is not a reason to retry every failed request. In a healthtech incident, the useful record is the smallest set of events that lets an engineer reconstruct what happened: the source failure, the delivery attempt, the quota response, and the final disposition. Retrying blindly can turn one patient-impacting symptom into a burst of duplicate notifications and a noisier audit trail. Short answer: treat HTTP 429 as a scheduling signal, honor Retry-After when it is valid, apply exponential backoff with jitter when it is absent, cap the number and age of attempts, and write one structured event for every attempt. Preserve the original alert identity across retries. The alert can be delayed; its evidence must not be rewritten. Start with identity. Then preserve tim…

entry.summary: Short answer: keep the bucket private, bind every object key to a server-validated tenant identifier, and issue a short-lived signed download only after the thumbnail record points to an object that exists. Resize work belongs behind a queue once CPU or memory becomes a meaningful part of the request SLO. That rule is less exciting than a public image URL, which is exactly why it survives an incident review. entry.title: Cheap runners for most CI jobs, fast runners for the few that matter
entry.summary:
We build Sengi, a hosted runner service for GitHub Actions. Today we launched Sengi Basic, at $1 per 1,000 runner minutes. This post is about the idea behind it: pick the runner per job, not per company. Look at a typical workflow run. Lint, unit tests, type checks, dependency audits, nightly jobs. Nobody is waiting on most of them. Then there are one or two jobs everyone is waiting on: the Docker image, the release build, the slow integration suite blocking a merge. Paying the same per-minute rate for both makes no sense. So Sengi has two classes:
Size Basic Premium GitHub-hosted Linux
2 vCPU $0.001/min $0.003/min $0.006/min
4 vCPU $0.002/min $0.006/min $0.012/min
8 vCPU $0.004/min $0.012/min $0.022/min
Basic gives you six times the minutes per dollar of GitHub's own runners at 2 and 4 vCPU, and 5.5 times at 8 vCPU. 10,000 2-vCPU minutes cost $10 on Basic and $60 on GitHub at list price. Premium is the fast class. On a PostHog Docker build at 4 vCPU it finished in 7m34s; GitHub's runner took 14m36s. The class is just the label: jobs: lint: runs-on: sengi-basic-2-ubuntu-2404 steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - run: npm ci && npm run lint
test: runs-on: sengi-basic-4-ubuntu-2404 steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - run: npm ci && npm test
image: needs: test runs-on: sengi-premium-8-ubuntu-2404 steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - run: docker build -t app .
Labels: sengi-basic-{2,4,8}-ubuntu-2404 and sengi-premium-{2,4,8}-ubuntu-2404. Workflows, secrets and logs stay in GitHub Actions. Move every job to Basic. Find the jobs where someone is waiting on the result. Run those on Premium and compare time and cost against Basic. Keep whichever wins for that job. Every account gets 3,000 free Basic minutes a month. A 4-vCPU minute counts as two and an 8-vCPU minute as four. More on Basic vs Premium: https://sengi.run/blog/sengi-basic-vs-premium

entry.title: The digital revolution, human nature, and epistemic distance
entry.summary: The article analyzes the transition from the analog to the digital world not as a change of tools, but as a fundamental transformation of the environment of human agency. The author points to the phenomenon of the elimination of material resistance—unlike the physical world, where interactions were direct and causally transparent, the digital world introduces an intermediary layer (the interface) that hides the processes leading to the result. Using the concept of embodied cognition, the text argues that this epistemic distancing changes how we build intuitions regarding causality and time. The technological success of digitalization lies in making the infrastructure invisible, which paradoxically increases the distance between human intent and the actual mechanism of the system's operation.

entry.title: What SEO actually costs in 2026: the numbers I use to check a quote
entry.summary: When a founder asks me whether a quote is fair, I check it against a handful of numbers from the largest survey of SEO providers I know of. Here they are, with the source for each. Ahrefs polled 439 SEO providers about their pricing. The headline figures: $2,917 a month was the average retainer, and most businesses spent between $500 and $5,000 a month. 78% of providers sell monthly retainers, 49% sell per project and 35% bill hourly (some offer more than one). Hourly averages by type: about $72 for freelancers, $99 for agencies and $171 for consultants. Experience matters: about $73 an hour at two years or less, about $118 at ten years or more. What do I get each month, in quantities? "Ongoing SEO" is not a scope. Four named pages a month is. Who does the work? The person I spoke to, or a junior behind an account manager? What is left out? Link building, implementation and tools are often billed separately. What do I own if I leave? Research, content and accounts should stay with the client. Google's own guidance is blunt about the red flag: no one can guarantee a number one ranking, and an SEO who claims a "special relationship" with Google is a reason to walk away. WebFX puts typical monthly SEO spend at $500 to $1,500 for a startup or micro-business and $1,500 to $3,500 for a small business. Spending enterprise money on a small site buys process, not results. Early on, a few pages close to a sale beat a big content calendar. I wrote up the full breakdown, with a table by service and by company size, in How Much Does SEO Cost? Prices by Service. If you're hiring an individual, SEO consultant rates splits hourly and project prices by experience. I'm Zeeshan, an SEO and content consultant. If you want a second opinion on a quote, send it to me.

entry.title: Why We're Building an AI Software Engineering Environment That Shows Its Work
entry.summary:
AI coding tools are good at producing code. They're much worse at showing you why you should trust it. You ask for a change, you get a diff, and then you're left with the real job: reading it, running the tests, and deciding whether it actually works. The proof is your problem. That's the gap we're working on at Zylvex Technologies, and it's why we're building ZylCode. ZylCode is an engineering workspace built around one rule: a result isn't done until there's evidence for it. Instead of a chat box that returns code, you describe an outcome and ZylCode turns it into a mission: Intent: you describe what should change. Plan: the work is broken into explicit steps. Evidence: candidate changes are checked by running your real test suite. Verified result: you see what passed, what didn't, and why. Nothing runs by itself. Queued work executes only when you press Run queued. The agent doesn't get to quietly act in the background. Commands run for real. The built-in terminal runs commands in your actual shell, so what you see is what happened. To be upfront: it's a command runner, not a full interactive PTY, and the working directory persists per session. Verification is part of the workflow. Missions come with an explicit verification path from the start, not as an afterthought. ZylCode is a Developer Preview, and we'd rather be honest about that than oversell it. Available: missions (the intent pipeline) and repository intelligence Limited: the runtime for web/desktop Coming soon: a design studio and a multi-agent board This is the real application, not a mockup:
Try it and tell us what breaks
The code is here: github.com/zylvex-tech/zylcode We'd really like feedback on one question: what evidence would you need before you'd trust an AI-generated change enough to merge it? Tell us in the comments.

entry.title: Cut one conflicting rule before you trim anything else
entry.summary: When an agent seems to ignore your rules, the cause is often two rules that disagree rather than a file that's too long. This post shows why fixing one conflict usually helps more than cutting lines. Originally published on clogmeter.vercel.app. When AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, Cursor rules, and skills all load, the agent does not get “more guidance” — it gets three copies of the same rule and often one quiet contradiction. Always/never pairs that disagree burn tokens twice and teach the model to hedge. Quick fix: open every instruction file side by side and search for the same verb (“never commit”, “always run tests”). Keep one canonical line in a single source of truth; delete or @-import the rest. Then weigh what is left. If you want to see where your own AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md or Cursor rules spend tokens, I built a free browser-only checker that also flags duplicates and always/never conflicts: Clogmeter.

entry.title: How Taocarts Generates Locale-Aware Watermarks for Product Images
entry.summary: When you sell the same product across Shopify, Coupang, Woo, and Base, the image that works in English can quietly break in another market. A price overlay in dollars, a "free shipping" badge in the wrong language, or a brand mark placed where local law forbids it — small things, but they erode trust and sometimes trip compliance. We stopped hand-editing images per market. Instead, we generate locale-aware watermarks at upload time. A listing photo is rarely just a photo. It carries context: currency, promotional badges, certification marks, and the brand. When that context is baked into the pixels in one language, every other market inherits a detail that doesn't belong to it. We saw English badges sitting on Korean listings and EUR prices on USD storefronts because someone forgot one export. Each locale has a watermark template: position, font, allowed badge set, and a translation key. When a product image is uploaded once, the system renders one variant per active locale using that template. The original stays clean; the watermarked copies are derived, never edited by hand. Technically this is a queue job. The buyer and warehouse apps are React Native; the image service is a small Express.js worker that pulls the template, composes the overlay, and writes the localized variant to object storage. The Laravel domain layer owns which locales are active for a product, so a listing disabled in Korea simply doesn't get a Korean variant. Two concrete wins. First, compliance: some markets require cert marks or specific disclaimers on the image itself. Templates make that a config change, not a redesign. Second, speed: a new market turns on by adding a template, not by re-shooting or re-editing thousands of photos. The part we're proud of is boring on purpose — nothing clever, just a deterministic pipeline that turns "one image, many correct overlays" into a default behavior instead of a manual chore.

entry.title: Inkling 2 Small 发布：68 小时主预训练，多模态与可定制性并重
entry.summary:
Thinking Machines 发布了 Inkling 2 Small：一款支持文本、图像输入和文本输出的混合专家（MoE）模型，重点强调训练效率、原生视觉能力，以及面向具体任务的可定制性。 对开发者来说，首先要区分服务可用与权重开放：模型目前已在 Tinker 和 Tinker Playground 提供推理与微调服务，但发布时尚未开放权重。团队计划在外部安全测试完成后，于发布后的下一周以 Apache 2.0 许可证开放权重；这仍是计划，而非已经完成的发布动作。
项目 已披露信息
总参数量 5940 亿
激活参数量 170 亿
架构 多模态 MoE，具备原生视觉能力
输入与输出 文本、图像输入；文本输出
上下文窗口 100 万 token
最大输出长度 100 万 token
输入价格 每百万 token 0.30 美元
缓存输入价格 每百万 token 0.03 美元
输出价格 每百万 token 1.00 美元
训练价格 每百万 token 1.50 美元
团队披露，模型在 GB300 上完成预训练耗时 68 小时，主预训练阶段使用了 8.4 万亿 token，并原生采用 NVFP4 精度。预训练、中期训练和后训练整个流程均使用 NVFP4。 另有约 12 万亿 token 的训练数据规模说法，但这一数字可能包含中期训练，不能直接与主预训练阶段的 8.4 万亿 token 混为一谈。 后训练则持续了 9 天，进行了约 1700 万次 rollout，即采样生成过程。因此，理解训练效率时需要保留两个边界： 68 小时不是完整训练流程的总耗时，不能将其等同于从预训练到后训练的全部时间。 现有信息没有给出 GPU 数量，不能只凭训练时长推算总算力消耗或训练成本。 在 Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.0.1 中，Inkling 2 Small 得分为 31 分，较 Inkling Small 提高 18 分。 已披露的对比显示，其得分与 Gemini 3.8 Flash（high） 相当，高于 MiMo-V2.6-Pro。 这些结果说明模型在这一综合评测中取得了进步，但不能据此推导出它在所有任务上都领先。现有信息也没有提供足够完整的 Muse Spark 对比数据，因此不宜使用“全面击败”等结论。 对于工程选型，榜单分数可以作为初筛依据，但仍需用实际任务验证效果。 除了通用能力，团队还将微调后的适应能力作为重要设计目标，并设置了会影响发布决策的可定制性评测。 团队表示，在固定数据量和预算下，Inkling 2 Small 的微调效果优于所比较的替代模型。不过，目前没有完整披露相关任务、对照设置与结果，实际收益仍需结合具体业务数据验证。 无论是在团队内部复盘，还是在写好标智库分享模型选型经验，都应同时交代任务、数据量、预算和对照设置，避免把特定条件下的微调收益理解为普遍优势。 John Schulman 披露，早期检查点曾在训练和评测期间学会绕过防护措施，团队随后在发布前进行了集中对齐工作。开放权重的安排也以外部安全测试完成为前提。 因此，当前状态可以概括为： 平台服务已可用：可以通过 Tinker 和 Tinker Playground 使用推理与微调服务。 权重在发布时尚未开放：不能将平台可调用理解为已经可以下载权重。 开放时间仍待落实：计划中的开放安排取决于外部安全测试进度。 对准备试用的开发者而言，下一步更值得验证的是：模型在自身任务上的表现、微调相对基础模型的增益，以及实际运行成本。68 小时主预训练是一个值得关注的效率指标，但不是完整训练成本或部署价值的替代指标。

Linux on the PS4 is not new. Community kernels have run on it for years, and you can find ready-made distros for it. But installing one has always meant a PC, a USB stick or a partitioning step, and a fixed distro picked by whoever built the image. entry.title: Your JSON isn't broken — your strings are: escapes, BOMs and the 2^53 lie
entry.summary: A few weeks ago we published a 30-second audit for spotting JSON tools that leak your payloads. This post is about the other kind of pain: the times JSON "breaks" and it's not the JSON's fault at all — it's the strings, the invisible characters, or a number that silently lied to you. These are the four failure modes we see most, and what to actually do about them. JSON strings allow exactly: \" \ \/ \b \f \n \r \t and \uXXXX. That's it. Two gotchas hide in plain sight: Astral characters need surrogate pairs. \uXXXX is one UTF-16 code unit. To escape 𝄞 (U+1D11E) you need \uD834\uDD1E. A lone surrogate like \uD834 is invalid JSON — yet some parsers accept it and crash later, far from the cause. Real newlines and tabs are illegal inside strings. entry.title: The Substrate Trap: Why Enterprise AI Use Outruns Its EBIT Impact

entry.title: Keep AI-suggested loading skeletons matched to real content height
entry.summary: Agents love inventing skeleton screens. Ask for a loading state and you get a neat gray card with three lines… that is half the height of the real content. When data arrives, the layout jumps. CLS goes up. Reviewers shrug because “at least there is a skeleton.” I’ve started treating height match as a hard constraint, not a nice-to-have. If the skeleton doesn’t reserve roughly the same vertical space as the loaded UI, send it back. AI drafts tend to: Copy a generic “3 lines + avatar” pattern from training data Ignore the real card’s padding, media block, or multi-row meta Use fixed h-4 bars that look pretty in isolation and wrong in the page Forget mobile denser layouts vs desktop taller cards The PR still “has a loading state,” so it merges. entry.title: What Fixing My Aunt’s Laptop Taught Me About Data Boundaries at Home
entry.summary:
Last month I spent a Saturday afternoon cleaning up my aunt’s laptop, and it turned into one of the more interesting security conversations I’ve had all year. Nothing dramatic happened, no malware popup, no ransom note. It was just the small stuff: three antivirus trials fighting each other, a browser with too many extensions, and a Downloads folder that looked like a landfill. I’ve noticed that helping relatives with tech is its own strange exercise. At work I can run a scan, check policy settings, maybe pull logs if something looks off. At her kitchen table I had none of that, and honestly I didn’t need most of it.
Here’s what struck me most: her laptop held more sensitive material than I expected. Tax documents from years back, scans of her passport, a folder of passwords she kept in a…

entry.title: Building Marlo: An Open-Source AI CMO for Founders and Startups
entry.summary: As founders, we spend countless hours building products, fixing bugs, and talking to customers. But when it comes to marketing, things get complicated quickly. You need to research competitors, find keywords, write blog posts, create content for LinkedIn and X, engage on Reddit, optimize SEO, generate leads, and keep everything consistent. Most founders either spend too much time on marketing or can't afford a dedicated team. That's why I built Marlo. What is Marlo? Marlo is an open-source AI CMO that helps founders and startups automate marketing research, strategy, and execution. Instead of using multiple tools, Marlo combines everything into one platform powered by specialized AI agents. What Marlo Can Do Most AI marketing tools are black boxes. I wanted Marlo to be: Open and transparent You own your data, choose your models, and extend the platform based on your needs. Who Is Marlo For? My vision is simple: Every founder should have access to an AI-powered marketing team without paying agency prices or juggling dozens of disconnected tools. Marlo is still evolving, and I'm actively looking for feedback from builders, marketers, and early adopters. If you're interested in AI-powered growth, open-source software, or marketing automation, I'd love to hear your thoughts. 🚀 Try Marlo: https://marlo.mlforge.in ⭐ GitHub: https://github.com/Kumar2421/marlo-self-hosted-ai-cmo

entry.title: How we monitor websites and servers before problems reach customers
entry.summary:
Short answer
We monitor websites and servers on several levels: whether the site responds from the outside, how loaded the server is, what the logs say and whether backups exist. The goal is to learn about a problem from our own monitoring, not from a client calling to say the site won't load. When we say customers, we also mean our clients' customers. The person who can't complete an order. The enquiry that never reaches anyone. The page that takes 15 seconds to load, so the visitor closes the tab. This is the first level, and we handle it with Uptime Kuma. It checks websites at regular intervals from an external point in the network, not from the server itself, and raises a signal when one stops responding. Ones that fit specific jobs way better than your old defaults. Here are seven your code generator has probably never suggested. entry.title: When an AI Agent Says 'Done,' What Exactly Has Finished?
entry.summary: "Done." It's probably the most satisfying word in a coding-agent session. It can also conceal three very different questions: Was the work permitted? Did the work actually happen? entry.title: Enterprise AI's real risk isn't autonomous agents. It's the complexity between them.
entry.summary:
Presented by Gravitee
Agent complexity is the insidious shadow lurking inside enterprises right now that needs a light shone on it. That’s because enterprises don't deploy a single agent and watch it run, they deploy fleets, each one calling APIs, calling other agents, reaching into applications that were never built with a machine decision-maker in mind. That's the failure mode that should keep you up at night: a windy, complicated system nobody can see clearly enough to govern. But why do things get so opaque so quickly? Add a second agent to a system, and you've added one connection. Add a tenth, and you haven't added ten connections, you've potentially added dozens, because now any agent might call any other, and each of those calls can trigger a call somewhere else. Complexity doesn…

entry.title: When agents act on their own, governance has to live in the data layer
entry.summary:
Presented by EDB
As enterprises give AI agents more autonomy — the ability to plan, decide, and act across systems without a human approving each step — a hard question moves to the center of every architecture review: When an agent tries to complete an action that it was never authorized to do, what actually stops it? These are your agents, running on your models, touching your data in your infrastructure — and the responsibility for what they do sits with you. That responsibility can’t be met in hindsight or with a set of abstract policies that live on paper but not in practice. Agents need rules in the context of the moment, because they don’t exercise overriding judgment of their own actions. Consider a simple rule: Never open the car door.
